title: [FlyDSL] [Bugfix] Route a16w4 SiLU MoE to CK-Tile and apply swiglu_limit
body:
## Motivation

A bf16-activation x MXFP4-weight SiLU MoE with a `swiglu_limit` has no working route. This is the small-batch path that DeepSeek-V4.1 takes on gfx950 whenever the token count is below `AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND` (default 256). `get_2stage_cfgs` only sends SwiGLU to CK-Tile there, so SiLU falls through to CK2stages. CK2stages has no A16W4 SiLU instance and no clamp. In our container the JIT build of `module_moe_ck2stages_b16_fp4x2_preshuffle_on_b16_silu_per_1x32_mulWeightStage2` fails at server start. Where it builds, `swiglu_limit` would be dropped.

Downstream, sgl-project/sglang#39857 carries this change as a Docker patch, and DeepSeek-V4.1 deployments set `AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND=0` to stay on the a8w4 route. This PR lets both go.

## Technical Details

- `get_2stage_cfgs`: SiLU with bf16 output on gate/up-interleaved MXFP4 weights takes the CK-Tile split-K post-activation route that SwiGLU already uses. SwiGLU keeps its `standard` post-activation layout; SiLU uses `auto`, which selects the interleaved FlyDSL activation for fp4 weights.
- `fused_moe_2stages`: forwards `swiglu_limit` to `cktile_moe_stage1` for that SiLU case.
- `cktile_moe_stage1` and `flydsl_silu_and_mul_interleaved`: take `swiglu_limit` and pass it to the kernel (`runtime_swiglu_limit`) instead of a fixed `inf`.
- The SiLU route is limited to `GateMode.INTERLEAVE`. On separated gate/up weights the output was about 4.5% (cosine) off the clamped reference, so that layout is left as it was.

## Test Plan

```bash
AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND=256 python -m pytest op_tests/test_moe_a16w4_silu_limit.py -q
```

The new test runs a DeepSeek-V4.1-shaped MoE (model_dim 5120, inter_dim 2304, 32 experts, top-6, `swiglu_limit=7`) through `fused_moe` and compares it with the clamped `torch_moe_stage1/2` reference. It also checks that the inputs actually reach the limit.

## Test Result

MI350X VF (gfx950), ROCm 10 Python wheels with torch 2.11. Current main does not JIT-build in this container (`module_moe_asm`), so the change was validated on `acf8fdf93`, where it applies unchanged.

| | token=1 | token=32 |
|---|---|---|
| without this change | JIT build failure | JIT build failure |
| with this change (cosine diff vs clamped ref) | 1.3e-5 | 1.4e-5 |

End to end, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash TP4 with the default bound serves and scores 0.910 on GSM8K (200 questions); without the change the server fails to start.

## Submission Checklist

- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [gfx950] pa_decode_sparse: pick BLOCK_K by occupancy, not a constant (up to +43 %)
body:
Fixes the fixed `BLOCK_K = 64` in the gfx950 sparse-decode driver, as described in #5293.

**What changes:** `BLOCK_K` is chosen after `num_splits` is known — 32 when the launch produces more CTAs than there are CUs, 64 otherwise. One comparison, no extra work.

**Why the grid size and not the query count:** the two are not proportional, because `num_splits` varies. 34 queries can launch more CTAs than 64 do, which is why the fastest tile width is not monotonic in `num_queries`. Sorted by CTA count it is monotonic, and the crossover sits exactly at `get_num_sms()`.

**Why it helps:** this kernel is neither bandwidth- nor compute-bound — on MI355X it reaches ~10 % of peak HBM bandwidth (even with fully contiguous indices, so it is not the gather pattern) and ~7 % of peak flops. It is latency-bound, so occupancy is what matters. The narrow tile uses 32 KB LDS instead of 64 KB and lets several CTAs share a CU.

**Measurements** (MI355X/gfx950, 64 heads, head_dim 512 = 448 NoPE + 64 RoPE, packed fp8 cache, top-k 2048, minimum of 5 rounds × 15 iterations):

| queries | fixed K=64 | this patch | delta | vs per-point optimum |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 63.2 µs | 62.6 µs | +0.9 % | −0.9 % |
| 24 | 78.3 | 72.9 | +7.4 % | +0.4 % |
| 32 | 73.4 | 73.4 | +0.1 % | −0.1 % |
| 48 | 121.3 | 109.7 | +10.6 % | +0.0 % |
| 64 | 131.0 | 131.1 | −0.1 % | +0.1 % |
| 96 | 218.0 | 193.8 | +12.5 % | +0.1 % |
| **128** | 264.6 | **185.4** | **+42.7 %** | +0.2 % |
| 192 | 402.8 | 355.2 | +13.4 % | +0.0 % |
| 256 | 550.2 | 392.4 | +40.2 % | −2.6 % |

Never worse than −0.6 % anywhere on the curve. **Numerics are unchanged** — max abs deviation against a torch reference is 0.000061 for both tile widths.

The rule also transfers unchanged to a 4-bit packed cache variant we tested locally (128 queries: 289.9 → 220.2 µs), so it is not specific to the fp8 layout.

**Things I measured that did not help**, in case it saves someone the search: `GSPT` 8 or 32 instead of 16 (−14 % / −45 %), `waves_per_eu` 1/2/4 (−4 % to −69 %), cache modifier `.cs` instead of `.cg` (does not compile), and forcing `kv_splits` (the automatic choice is already optimal at 64+ queries; more splits cost up to 45 %).

Happy to re-measure on other shapes — different head counts, top-k values, or a bf16 cache — if that would help review.

title: [HIP] [Perf] Specialize partial tiles in two-stage custom all-reduce
body:
## Proposed modifications

1. Specialize the plain two-stage read kernel with a compile-time `has_tail` parameter.
2. Run the shared-memory loop only over complete tiles so every thread in a block executes the same number of barriers.
3. Reduce leftover packs directly with `packed_reduce`, preserving their original owner threads and output indices.
4. Preserve accumulation order and inter-device synchronization without adding a kernel launch.
5. Dispatch aligned messages to `has_tail=false`, removing tail predicates and restoring the generated aligned kernel from before #5694.
6. Keep #5694's write-mode and fused-kernel fixes intact, along with the existing naive handling of unequal rank partitions and TP6.
7. Add a Gloo-based regression with independent rank inputs, exact reference sums, and changing inputs in eager and graph execution.
8. Cover graph-owned intermediate registration, poisoned replay outputs, the reported shape and its neighbors, single-lane tails, and unequal partitions.
9. Include the flattened `(1023,512)`, `(1024,512)`, and `(1025,512)` cases in the existing default benchmark sweep, keeping the list sorted, deduplicated, and within its configured size cutoff.

## Microbenchmarks and performance comparison

This follows merged #5694 and targets current `main`; it preserves that PR's correctness fixes while specializing the plain read path. The benchmark study used four gfx950 GPUs at TP4 and a common `v0.1.22.post1` base (`b4d9154d125e09efbe098d986e40fea3549c1244`). The correct comparison baseline applied #5694's three barrier hunks (`5e77166e0c627caa109046f6469de8220efa5ba6`) to that base. These are the historical isolated-kernel measurements, not a newly timed end-to-end run of current `main`.

The study completed 44 variant runs: three alternating-order rounds for focused and broad sweeps, and five for eight additional BF16 shapes. Each case used five warmups and seven samples: 64 calls per eager sample, or 64 captured calls replayed ten times per graph sample. CUDA-event timing excludes input preparation and checking; eager results include Python launch/allocation gaps. Latencies are the median across rounds of each round's maximum per-rank sample median. Percentage changes are medians of paired within-round ratios and need not equal ratios of the displayed latencies.

For `(1025, 512)`, lower latency is better:

| Dtype | Mode | #5694 uniform loop (µs) | Tail specialization (µs) | Paired change |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 | eager | 16.461 | 16.330 | -0.90% |
| BF16 | graph | 13.822 | 13.722 | -0.72% |
| FP16 | eager | 16.440 | 16.254 | -0.94% |
| FP16 | graph | 13.831 | 13.678 | -0.95% |
| FP32 | eager | 26.883 | 26.753 | -0.02% |
| FP32 | graph | 24.001 | 23.898 | -0.48% |

The full sweep includes BF16/FP16/FP32 at `(1023,512)`, `(1024,512)`, and `(1025,512)`; 43 dtype/size configurations spanning 8 KiB–8 MiB and per-rank tails of 1/63/64/65/127 packs; and BF16 `(M,2880)` for `M=120,121,127,157,160,161,256,512`. Compared with the unsafe pre-#5694 release, the proposed specialization's largest observed case-level median increases were 0.56% graph and 1.92% eager; the initial whole-message naive fallback cost about 29% on the reported BF16 graph case. The unsafe release is a historical timing reference only.

The host was shared, the other four GPUs were busy, and three to five rounds do not establish a general sub-percent regression bound. Timed graph replays reuse inputs within a sample; the separate changing-input regression provides stronger race coverage. TP8/gfx942 configurations and end-to-end model throughput were not measured. This PR keeps the upstream write-mode dispatch, including its partial-tile handling.

## Validation

The previously tested tail specialization passed 8,400 changing-input checks per rank at TP4 across BF16/FP16/FP32 and 600 per rank at TP2. The unmodified vLLM PR #58433 test file passed all four BF16/MXFP8 TP2/TP4 cases in 74.15 seconds. The unsafe release failed the reported shape at eager iteration 0, with 125 mismatches and a maximum absolute error of 22. The actual main-based branch and pristine `main` both clean-built for gfx950. All 48 gfx950 specialized read-kernel variants match the previously tested tail kernels byte-for-byte, including resource metadata; all 24 current-main read variants match the benchmarked #5694 baseline. All 24 PR write-kernel variants match pristine main. On the actual current-main PR branch, BF16/FP16/FP32 TP4 each passed six shapes with 100 eager and 100 graph iterations per shape. The unmodified vLLM integration suite passed again: **4 passed in 71.75 seconds**, covering BF16/MXFP8 at TP2/TP4. Ruff, Black, Python syntax, and diff checks passed.

Follow-up validation repeated the unchanged vLLM test group in **50 fresh pytest processes: 200/200 cases passed**, with zero failures, errors, skips, timeouts, or retries (68.2 minutes). Six runs emitted TCPStore shutdown warnings while all tests passed. The kernel and compiled collective library are unchanged by the benchmark-list follow-up.

The three boundary sizes also passed **18/18 cases through the existing benchmark** at TP4: BF16/FP16/FP32 in eager and graph modes. Profiler records confirmed the intended two-stage tail specialization for both neighbors and the aligned specialization for the middle size on all four ranks; 21 size-list/cutoff checks passed. These benchmark checks use the existing random-input tolerance. The default sweep now includes these shapes without `-s`, for example:

```bash
python op_tests/multigpu_tests/test_custom_allreduce.py -t 4 -d bf16 -m graph
```

Regression command (repeat for `fp16` and `fp32`):

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 python op_tests/multigpu_tests/test_custom_allreduce.py \
    --regression -t 4 -d bf16 --iterations 100
```

<details>
<summary>Standalone microbenchmark reproducer</summary>

Build/install each revision using the repository's usual source-build instructions, save the following as `bench_allreduce_tail.py`, and run it against each revision. The output records the loaded collective library's SHA256, per-rank timings, and correctness results. Alternate revision order between repeated runs.

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 python bench_allreduce_tail.py \
    --output latency.json --case-set all --dtypes bf16 fp16 fp32 \
    --modes eager graph --calls 64 --replays 10 --samples 7 --warmup 5
```

```python
"""Direct AITER TP4 latency/correctness study; host coordination uses Gloo."""

import argparse
import datetime
import hashlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import platform
import socket
import statistics
import time


def cases_for(args):
    cases = []
    for dtype in args.dtypes:
        element_size = 4 if dtype == "fp32" else 2
        candidates = []
        if args.case_set in ("all", "regression"):
            candidates += [(f"shape_{m}x512", (m, 512)) for m in (1023, 1024, 1025)]
        if args.case_set in ("all", "representative"):
            candidates += [(f"bytes_{n}", (n // element_size,))
                           for n in (8192, 65536, 262144, 524288, 1048576, 4194304, 8388608)]
        if args.case_set in ("all", "boundary"):
            candidates += [(f"tile_boundary_{offset:+}", ((1048576 + offset) // element_size,))
                           for offset in (-64, 0, 64, 63 * 64, 64 * 64, 65 * 64)]
        if args.case_set == "upstream":
            candidates += [(f"upstream_{m}x2880", (m, 2880))
                           for m in (120, 121, 127, 157, 160, 161, 256, 512)]
        seen = set()
        for name, shape in candidates:
            numel = 1
            for n in shape:
                numel *= n
            if numel in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(numel)
            cases.append({"name": name, "dtype": dtype, "shape": shape,
                          "bytes": numel * element_size, "numel": numel,
                          "full_packed_tile": numel * element_size % (512 * 16) == 0})
    return cases


def worker(rank, port, args):
    import torch
    import torch.distributed as dist
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
    device = torch.device("cuda", rank)
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", init_method=f"tcp://127.0.0.1:{port}",
                            rank=rank, world_size=4,
                            timeout=datetime.timedelta(seconds=60))
    from aiter.dist.device_communicators.custom_all_reduce import CustomAllreduce
    from aiter.jit import core
    ar = None
    report = {"config": vars(args), "results": []}
    try:
        ar = CustomAllreduce(dist.group.WORLD, device, max_size=16 * 1024 * 1024)
        assert not ar.disabled
        collective = Path(core.get_module("module_custom_all_reduce").__file__)
        report["metadata"] = {
            "python": platform.python_version(), "torch": torch.__version__,
            "device": torch.cuda.get_device_name(rank),
            "arch": torch.cuda.get_device_properties(rank).gcnArchName,
            "visible_devices": os.environ.get("HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES"),
            "collective": str(collective),
            "collective_sha256": hashlib.sha256(collective.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
        }
        dtype_map = {"bf16": torch.bfloat16, "fp16": torch.float16, "fp32": torch.float32}
        cases = cases_for(args)
        # Alternate case order as well as variant order across paired rounds.
        if args.reverse_cases:
            cases.reverse()
        for case in cases:
            x = torch.empty(case["shape"], dtype=dtype_map[case["dtype"]], device=device)
            indices = torch.arange(case["numel"], dtype=torch.int32, device=device).reshape(case["shape"])

            def set_input(seed):
                local = ((indices * (rank + 1) + seed * (rank + 3)) % 31) - 15
                x.copy_(local)
                ref = sum((((indices * (r + 1) + seed * (r + 3)) % 31) - 15)
                          for r in range(4))
                return ref.to(x.dtype)

            def check(outputs, expected):
                # Check every captured call: racing intermediate outputs also count.
                mismatch = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
                max_error = torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
                finite = torch.ones((), dtype=torch.bool, device=device)
                for out in outputs:
                    mismatch += torch.count_nonzero(out != expected)
                    finite &= torch.isfinite(out).all()
                    max_error = torch.maximum(max_error, (out.float() - expected.float()).abs().max())
                return {"mismatches": mismatch.item(), "finite": finite.item(),
                        "max_abs_error": max_error.item()}

            for mode in args.modes:
                expected = set_input(1)
                for _ in range(args.warmup):
                    warm = ar.custom_all_reduce(x)
                    assert warm is not None
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
                dist.barrier()
                graph = None
                outputs = []
                if mode == "graph":
                    stream = torch.cuda.Stream()
                    stream.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
                    graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
                    with ar.capture():
                        with torch.cuda.graph(graph, stream=stream):
                            outputs = [ar.custom_all_reduce(x) for _ in range(args.calls)]
                    torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(stream)
                    for _ in range(args.warmup):
                        graph.replay()
                    torch.cuda.synchronize()
                    dist.barrier()

                timings = []
                wall_timings = []
                correctness = []
                start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
                end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
                for sample in range(args.samples):
                    expected = set_input(100 + sample)
                    if mode == "graph":
                        for out in outputs:
                            out.fill_(float("nan"))
                    torch.cuda.synchronize()
                    dist.barrier()
                    before = time.perf_counter()
                    start.record()
                    if mode == "graph":
                        for _ in range(args.replays):
                            graph.replay()
                        n_ops = args.calls * args.replays
                    else:
                        outputs = [ar.custom_all_reduce(x) for _ in range(args.calls)]
                        n_ops = args.calls
                    end.record()
                    end.synchronize()
                    wall_timings.append((time.perf_counter() - before) * 1e6 / n_ops)
                    timings.append(start.elapsed_time(end) * 1000 / n_ops)
                    correctness.append(check(outputs, expected))
                    dist.barrier()

                local = {"rank": rank, "samples_us": timings,
                         "median_us": statistics.median(timings),
                         "wall_samples_us": wall_timings,
                         "correctness": correctness}
                gathered = [None] * 4
                dist.all_gather_object(gathered, local)
                if rank == 0:
                    result = {**case, "mode": mode, "ranks": gathered,
                              "max_rank_median_us": max(r["median_us"] for r in gathered),
                              "exact": all(c["mismatches"] == 0 for r in gathered for c in r["correctness"]),
                              "finite": all(c["finite"] for r in gathered for c in r["correctness"])}
                    report["results"].append(result)
                    destination = Path(args.output)
                    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                    temporary = destination.with_suffix(".tmp")
                    temporary.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n")
                    temporary.replace(destination)
                    print(f"RESULT {case['dtype']} {case['name']} {mode} "
                          f"us={result['max_rank_median_us']:.4f} "
                          f"exact={result['exact']} finite={result['finite']}", flush=True)
                del outputs, graph
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
                dist.barrier()
            del x, indices, expected, warm
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        dist.barrier()
    finally:
        if ar is not None:
            ar.close()
        dist.destroy_process_group()


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--dtypes", nargs="+", choices=("bf16", "fp16", "fp32"),
                        default=["bf16", "fp16", "fp32"])
    parser.add_argument("--modes", nargs="+", choices=("eager", "graph"), default=["eager", "graph"])
    parser.add_argument("--case-set", choices=("all", "regression", "representative", "boundary", "upstream"), default="all")
    parser.add_argument("--calls", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--replays", type=int, default=10)
    parser.add_argument("--samples", type=int, default=7)
    parser.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--reverse-cases", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--list-cases", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    assert min(args.calls, args.replays, args.samples, args.warmup) > 0
    return args


if __name__ == "__main__":
    args = parse_args()
    if args.list_cases:
        print(json.dumps(cases_for(args), indent=2))
    else:
        import torch.multiprocessing as mp
        with socket.socket() as sock:
            sock.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
            port = sock.getsockname()[1]
        mp.spawn(worker, args=(port, args), nprocs=4, join=True)
```

</details>

## History and motivation

This work began when [vLLM PR #58433](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58433) intermittently failed TP4 tests in [Buildkite build #90750](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/90750) despite passing on retry. The `(1025, 512)` case exposed block barriers inside a loop whose iteration count differed between threads at a partial tile. A local regression reproduced corruption in the original release. Routing partial messages to the naive kernel restored correctness but increased BF16 graph latency by about 29%. Merged [AITER PR #5694](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/5694) fixes the barrier defect with uniform loop bounds. This follow-up retains its write-mode and fused fixes while specializing complete tiles and leftover packs in the plain read kernel. The motivation is to preserve the correctness fix with minimal performance cost and keep the original test shapes and assertions.

AI assistance was used for implementation, investigation, and validation.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [HIP] [JIT] Add opt-in M3 sequence-parallel collectives and tiled MoE sorting
body:
The M3 sequence-parallel path needs contiguous reduction shards, attention outputs in token-major head layout, and faster sorting of large prefill batches. This adds the AITER kernels used by [ROCm/ATOM#2364](https://github.com/ROCm/ATOM/pull/2364) to reduce communication and layout-processing overhead.

- Add four-rank INT4 QuickReduce reduce-scatter for contiguous FP16/BF16 tensors. It reuses the existing codec and communicator state, sends one data phase, and protects IPC-buffer reuse with a consumption barrier. Calls sharing a communicator must remain serialized on its current stream.
- Add four-rank head exchange that writes the final token-major head layout directly, using CustomAllreduce registered pointers and synchronization. It supports staged inputs and already-registered graph inputs.
- Add opt-in tiled MoE sorting with stable packed token IDs, expert padding, and optional auxiliary mappings. `use_tiled_sort` defaults to `False`; the dispatch guard targets gfx950 M3 MXFP4 prefill with 32,768 tokens, top-k 5, 129 experts, hidden size 6,144, intermediate size 768, and block size 64. Unsupported contracts, including caller-provided output buffers, use the existing dispatcher. Launch settings use the shared JSON config loader, and kernels include config-aware trace names.

This reuses the existing norm/quantization kernels and leaves existing QuickAllReduce entry points unchanged. The sorting implementation is a separate histogram/prefix/stable-scatter algorithm; the original four sorting phases remain valid.

### Validation

Rebased onto `11d38524cb12d4ff56fa89c2b03418afcc78c41c`. On four gfx950 GPUs:

- **32/32 GPU sorting tests passed**, including exact packed-route/padding/auxiliary output, changed-input graph replay, fallback behavior, and byte-exact M3 fused-MoE output comparison. The companion ATOM four-rank transport/GQA/graph and MXFP4 prequantization/MoE checks also passed.
- The full SP model ran with `3e3a168a8e3476e7fd5731e48c32341540d98c07`; all four workers loaded the fresh QuickRS and head-exchange extensions. A clean-build failure caused by include ordering was fixed before this run.
- M3 **131072 input / 100 output / C16**, 16 warmups and 160 measured requests: optimized SP4 **43.221 output tok/s**, compared with **41.072** for TP4 QuickReduce all-reduce INT4 with BF16-to-FP16 cast (**+5.23%**). Both completed 160/160 requests with exact requested lengths and no errors. One measured run per configuration; this is combined system performance, not an isolated attribution to each kernel. Decode median ITL remains slower: **14.626 ms** versus **10.390 ms**.
- Full GSM8K, 1,319 samples, 5-shot: strict and flexible exact match **0.93783169**, above the requested **0.93** threshold. INT4 reduction is lossy; this is empirical model-quality acceptance.
- Python/C++ formatting, Ruff, Python compilation, JSON parsing, and 10 isolated CPU dispatcher/signature/config checks passed.

The TP4 run used `f2bd394f7`; the only subsequent AITER change restores required include ordering in the new QuickRS translation unit, which TP4 does not use. Both full-model runs used ATOM `cc7558ac` and the same benchmark client from ATOM `3a2df1d3`. The final ATOM branch was then rebased onto newer main with its M3 server runtime verified byte-identical; these numbers do not measure the new CI telemetry harness. The companion ATOM PR contains the full model settings and opt-in environment recipe.

The final CI follow-up only regroups imports in the benchmark script. Production kernel bodies and launch settings match the full-model run. Ruff 0.16.8 was rechecked without its cache.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [JIT] [Feature] Add tuned native group32 A8W8 Triton GEMM for gfx950
body:
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash projections use unshuffled E4M3 weights and compact E8M0 group32 scales. This adds a gfx950 Triton backend for those operands to `gemm_a8w8_blockscale`, together with tuned configurations for TP4, TP2 and attention-DP local GEMMs.

### Implementation and dispatch

- Keep activations, weights and scales in their native formats. Support compact 32x32 or per-row 1x32 weight scales, FP32 accumulation, and BF16/FP16/FP32 output.
- Use native microscaling MFMA, packed-K execution for small M, and the existing non-atomic split-K reduction. The public interface accepts an optional native-group32 `split_k` partition count, preserving explicit caller controls while keeping configured backend selection first.
- Query `get_CKGEMM_config` before selecting a fallback. Native E8M0 operands have a separate `AITER_CONFIG_GEMM_A8W8_BLOCKSCALE_GROUP32` CSV family, so an identical M/N/K in the FP32 128x128 table cannot select an incompatible kernel. Unsupported configured backends raise instead of silently falling back.
- Add 450 DSV4.1 model-config rows: 18 geometries and 25 M buckets, all selecting `libtype=triton`. Tile, split-K and packed-variant settings remain in the existing Triton JSON configuration system. Of these rows, 262 reuse exact-shape measured timings; remaining timing fields are empty.
- Extend the shared GEMM loader with optional file-defined `M_BOUNDS`, retaining explicit-argument precedence and legacy bounds. Config copies preserve nested mutation isolation while avoiding per-scalar `deepcopy` overhead.

The new native backend requires gfx950. Existing FP32 128x128 operands retain their CK/CKTile paths. Group32 currently supports the Triton backend; configuring legacy CK/CKTile for its E8M0 operands is rejected.

### Performance

Hardware: AMD gfx950, 256 CUs; PyTorch 2.9.1 ROCm 7.1.1 and Triton 3.8.0 ROCm build. Measurements use BF16 output, CUDA graphs and at least 512 MiB of rotating weights. The baseline is the initial imported native group32 configuration in the first commit of this PR.

The sweep evaluated 49,304 candidates across 234 representative M/N/K cases and validated 603 cases, including interval boundaries. The geometric-mean speedup is **1.179x** (15.18% lower GEMM latency). Of 300 intervals checked, 252 use improved configurations and 48 retain the baseline. The largest sampled slowdown among changed configurations is 0.97%. Measurements affected by other GPU users were discarded and rerun on available cards.

| Projection | N | K | Geometric-mean speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| qkv_a | 1792 | 5120 | 1.366x |
| indexer_q | 4096 | 1280 | 1.211x |
| q_b TP4 | 8192 | 1280 | 1.061x |
| q_b TP2 | 16384 | 1280 | 1.063x |
| q_b attention-DP | 32768 | 1280 | 1.112x |
| o_b TP4 | 5120 | 2048 | 1.188x |
| o_b TP2 | 5120 | 4096 | 1.221x |
| o_b attention-DP | 5120 | 8192 | 1.121x |
| shared_up TP4 | 1152 | 5120 | 1.131x |
| shared_up TP2 | 2304 | 5120 | 1.217x |
| shared_up TP1 | 4608 | 5120 | 1.194x |
| shared_down TP4 | 5120 | 576 | 1.273x |
| shared_down TP2 | 5120 | 1152 | 1.268x |
| shared_down TP1 | 5120 | 2304 | 1.243x |
| Engram | 25600 | 6144 | 1.123x |
| draft_main | 5120 | 15360 | 1.180x |
| draft_kv_fused | 1536 | 5120 | 1.176x |
| draft_kv | 512 | 5120 | 1.146x |

These are standalone GEMM results. End-to-end serving throughput was not measured. Tuning covers M through 4096; larger M retains the original JSON fallback. Model CSV entries through M=16384 choose the backend without claiming newly tuned tiles at those larger sizes.

### Validation

- **136 AITER tests passed** on the rebased branch: native numerical contracts, column/K tails, extreme scale codes, per-row scales, split-K, output buffers, live-input graph replay, dynamic-M fullgraph compile, CSV format isolation, and configured-backend precedence. CK/CKTile dispatch-priority tests use stubs; native numerical and graph tests execute GPU kernels.
- **100 ATOM integration tests passed** with the companion migration to the public AITER interface, covering actual backend-config lookup, blockscale projections, accumulation, GPU quantization, graph replay and dynamic batched fullgraph compilation.
- All **294,912** combinations of the 18 model geometries and integer M=1..16384 resolve through the real shared loader to Triton; unknown geometries still miss the table and reach fallback.
- Six representative cases comparing dispatch before/after the configuration-priority change have bitwise-equal BF16/FP32 outputs, identical GPU kernel sequences, and graph-latency differences below 0.5%.
- Black and Ruff pass for all seven changed Python files; `git diff --check` passes.

The sweep compares sampled outputs against an independent FP64 reference and complete BF16 outputs against the baseline. BF16 outputs are bitwise equal in 384/603 cases; the maximum BF16 relative RMS difference is 1.052e-4. One pre-existing FP32 reference-boundary outlier at M=97, N=5120, K=1152 remains: maximum absolute error changes from 0.09451294 to 0.09445190. The experiment accepts that point only when candidate error does not exceed baseline error; repository test tolerances are unchanged.

```bash
# AITER, on gfx950
python -m pytest -q \
  op_tests/test_gemm_group32_interface.py \
  op_tests/test_opus_a8w8_interface.py \
  op_tests/triton_tests/gemm/basic/test_gemm_a8w8_blockscale_group32.py

# ATOM integration, with the V4.1 reference weights available
ATOM_DSV41_REFERENCE=/mnt/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash python -m pytest -q \
  tests/model_ops/test_blockscale_packed.py \
  tests/models/deepseek_v41/test_accumulation.py \
  tests/models/deepseek_v41/test_quant_gpu.py
```

title: [Config] [Perf] Add DeepSeek V4.1 Flash TP4 gfx950 MoE tuning
body:
## Summary

Add 16 gfx950 tuning rows for the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash TP4 backbone and draft MoE shapes. These shapes currently have no exact entries in the shipped tuning tables and use heuristic FlyDSL configurations.

## Configuration

- H5120; TP-local logical intermediate 576, padded to 640.
- Backbone: 384 experts, top6; draft: 128 experts, top3; expert parallelism disabled.
- Token buckets 8/16/32/64/128/256/512/1024 for each geometry. Actual tested decode rows were backbone M6/12/24/48/96/192/384/768 and draft M5/10/20/40/80/160/320/640.
- BF16 output, FP8 activations, MXFP4 weights, per-1x32 scaling, interleaved gate/up, SiLU and no stage-one routing-weight multiplication.
- Existing unfused stage-one N128 kernels with M16/M32 tiles; stage-two N128/N256. Exact names and `ksplit=-1` are in the CSV.

The model-specific table contains only the 16 new keys, with explicit `gfx950`. Existing rows are unchanged. Kernel timing/error columns are blank: the measurements below include the complete local shared/routed MoE and TP collective, so they are not valid stage-one/stage-two kernel timings.

## Performance on the measured runtime

MI355X, TP4, Torch 2.12.0+rocm10.0.0, HIP 7.15.26333, Triton 3.8.0, AITER 0.1.21.post1 with the merged sorter fix from #5295. `AITER_BF16_FP8_MOE_BOUND=0`, fusion and routed-first scheduling disabled. This explicitly measures the A8W4 path; the CSV does not change activation-dtype selection policy.

Seeded synthetic weights/inputs, warm repeated routes, native shared-first MoE including gating, quantization, shared expert, routed expert and BF16 TP4 RCCL. Each of 31 alternating paired measurements takes the maximum rank latency over 16 graph replays. The other four GPUs were idle during confirmation.

| Concurrency | Backbone baseline → tuned (µs) | Median paired reduction | Draft baseline → tuned (µs) | Median paired reduction |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 105.44 → 100.99 | 4.28% | 77.21 → 75.61 | 2.22% |
| 2 | 148.98 → 136.65 | 8.30% | 89.36 → 86.54 | 3.20% |
| 4 | 175.62 → 168.02 | 4.43% | 116.18 → 113.09 | 2.56% |
| 8 | 253.40 → 246.09 | 2.89% | 145.83 → 140.55 | 3.50% |
| 16 | 342.17 → 332.31 | 2.95% | 176.08 → 170.67 | 3.11% |
| 32 | 429.24 → 417.17 | 2.82% | 195.88 → 193.00 | 1.42% |
| 64 | 524.29 → 512.66 | 2.20% | 265.47 → 258.08 | 2.77% |
| 128 | 584.40 → 577.08 | 1.24% | 316.79 → 309.12 | 2.42% |

The percentage is the median paired gain, so it need not equal the ratio of the two median times. All 16 target shapes passed the predeclared independent native-CSV gate: ≥1% median paired improvement and ≥25/31 faster pairs. Observed wins were 30/31 or 31/31. Earlier isolated selection also used an identical-kernel control to reject capture/timing bias.

## Validation and limits

- The original native CSV lookup resolved all 16 expected kernel pairs, without metadata overrides. Each geometry also passed M31/32/33/255/256/257 boundary checks.
- Eager and changed-input graph checks covered original, changed-input, concentrated-routing and restored-input cases. Fixed per-rank `atol=rtol=.02`, explicit FP64 local error budgets, propagated FP32 TP-sum budgets, input preservation and finite timed outputs passed. Strict FP32/BF16 aggregate parity diagnostics include mismatches and are retained separately; this is not a claim of bitwise or independent full-model accuracy.
- The benchmark retained one capture stream and diagnostic graphs/output buffers until synchronized cleanup after reproducing a graph-lifetime fault. No kernel arithmetic or scheduling change is included here.
- N64 stage-one variants were excluded because the investigated padded path left part of the intermediate unwritten.
- Full-model accuracy, every shape inside each lookup bucket, and GPU execution/serving throughput on this branch's current upstream runtime have **not** been validated. A short serving comparison on the measured private runtime is reported below.

Measured source identities include `moe_kernels.py` SHA256 `c6898ef73fa21fd519593592c511b29ae41443e3e753ce6165bc866271c2bd73` and `mixed_moe_gemm_2stage_common.py` SHA256 `bba3e08a6ac16c2106a8bde9b06a98aea6fb0c7764117b2630a3a091265e1853`. Upstream base `b0ced008d89f3fe8ad9fa9388d78b615fd53cb0b` has newer FlyDSL/LDS and stage-two addressing code. All 10 selected kernel names still register with identical parameters, but that CPU check does not establish equivalent performance or correctness on the newer implementation.

### Short serving follow-up (measured private runtime)

A matched TP4 controlled-decode check used 350,000 input tokens and 512 output tokens per request, two warmup batches and five measured batches at each concurrency, with synthetic speculative acceptance 3.51. The comparison uses the saved untuned baseline from a separate server lifetime. The tuned MoE CSV was selected; dense GEMM configuration, shared-first scheduling and unfused arithmetic were unchanged.

| Concurrency | Output tokens/s/chip, baseline → tuned | Throughput change | Mean server TPOT change |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 63.457 → 62.826 | -0.99% | +1.36% |
| 4 | 180.454 → 180.968 | +0.28% | -0.74% |
| 16 | 349.840 → 349.711 | -0.04% | -0.12% |
| 32 | 428.890 → 424.609 | -1.00% | -2.00% |

These short measurements show **no clear overall serving-throughput gain**, despite the isolated MoE gains above. All 20 measured batches completed with matching prompts, zero preemptions and no harness validation issues. TPOT is the server's mean time per output token, not p90 ITL. Synthetic acceptance and request completion do not establish model quality. This does not replace the still-pending current-upstream GPU validation; the PR remains a draft.

Command: `sudo -n /home/amd/vllm/.venv/bin/python dsv41_rocm_bench/moe_tuned_serving_20260917/run_short_verification.py --execute`. Both client/analyzer completed successfully and owned server cleanup completed without forced termination. Detailed local artifacts: `dsv41_rocm_bench/moe_tuned_serving_20260917/short_controlled_decode/{comparison.json,SHORT_COMPARISON.md}`.

### Commands run

On the measured runtime, the artifact-local `run_native_confirmation_v5.py` harness ran each TP4 lane with `--timing`, all eight actual shapes and six boundaries; both controllers exited zero and all four rank reports completed. `qualify_native_csv.py` checked all 16 rows against disjoint tuning/native reports and source hashes. A separate native metadata lookup checked the final combined CSV. These benchmark artifacts are outside this CSV-only patch.

On this upstream checkout:

```bash
git diff --cached --check
bash .githooks/install
.git/hooks/pre-commit
/home/amd/vllm/.venv/bin/python op_tests/tuning_tests/test_csv_validation.py TestCSVValidation.test_flydsl_stage2_sort_block_matches_fmoe_config
```

The CSV layout test passed. CPU checks also confirmed 16 unique new keys, no collisions with shipped tables, unchanged qualified row contents and identical registry parameters for all 10 selected names. No GPU was launched for upstream preparation.

## Related work

Open PR #5562 targets DSV4.1 **EP4** with H5120/I2304, 96 local experts and top5. This table targets **TP4** with H5120/I640, E384/top6 and E128/top3, so its lookup keys are distinct. Open-PR searches for DSV4.1, `640 fmoe`, and `fmoe CSV` found no proposal for these exact keys. #5315 addresses explicit architecture fields across existing tables; this new table already supplies `gfx950`.

AI assistance was used to prepare the tuning harness, analyze results, and draft this CSV change and description.

</details>

## Validation

- All 69 final cases completed with native baseline/candidate selection checked against the full CSVs. Eager calls, captured graph outputs, changed/stressed/restored inputs, finite outputs and unchanged inputs/weights were checked.
- Every checked element passed `atol=rtol=0.02` against the rounded FP32 reference and native baseline; no mismatch fraction was allowed. `err_ratio=0` records the observed mismatch fraction under those checks, not bit-exact output. The native BF16 tuner uses the looser `.05/.05` tolerance.
- CPU publication audit passed: all old rows and measured source files preserved, exact kernel selections and timing metadata reproduced, native config discovery checked, no duplicate keys or expanded retained lookup domains.
- Existing `TestConfigShapeCollision.test_bf16`, `test_selfcheck_detects_planted_duplicate`, and `test_selfcheck_passes_on_clean`: **3 passed, 0 skipped**. Executed with `.venv/bin/python` through a local unittest runner that verifies imported source paths, under a private `/tmp` mount.
- `bash .githooks/pre-commit` and `git diff --cached --check`: passed for the CSV-only change.

This is a bounded synthetic kernel benchmark. Full-model accuracy and end-to-end serving gains have not been measured. CSV `bw` is the conventional effective BF16 bytes/time calculation, not measured DRAM traffic.

## Related work

Open PRs were checked by title/body and relevant CSV diffs on 2026-09-17. No overlapping keys were found, including #4203, #4222, #5353 and #5602. #4663 uses N129280/K7168; these rows use K256. #3836 targets FP32 outputs. #5159 removes different GPT-OSS bias-enabled rows. The MoE configuration work in #5609 is a separate operator.

AI assistance was used for tuning automation, validation analysis and this description.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Fused Qwen3-Next GDN decode op for gfx950
body:
# [Triton/Gluon] Fused Qwen3-Next GDN decode op for gfx950

## Motivation

Qwen3-Next's Gated DeltaNet decode step runs as four separate kernels today:

```
fused_qkvzba_split_reshape_cat  ->  causal_conv1d_update
  ->  fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode  ->  gated RMSNorm
```

aiter has all the pieces for GDN — `chunk_gated_delta_rule`,
`fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule`, `causal_conv1d_update_split_qkv`,
`gated_rmsnorm_fp8_group_quant` — but **not the single-launch fusion**, and not
one that consumes the packed `qkvz`/`ba` projections directly.

This adds that op. On 4x MI355X / TP4 with Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 it is
worth **+6.0% to +9.1% end-to-end output throughput** when wired into SGLang
(companion PR), with no accuracy regression.

### Why a new op rather than a mode on `fused_kda_decode`

`fused_kda_decode` is the same *shape* of fusion — conv, recurrence, gated norm,
one launch — but it implements **KDA**, and the differences are structural, not
parametric:

| | `fused_kda_decode` | this op |
|---|---|---|
| head topology | one `H`; q/k/v all `H` heads | `VH == 2*KH` |
| gate | `lower_bound * sigmoid(exp(A)*(a+dt))`, vector over K | `exp(-exp(A_log)*softplus(a+dt))`, scalar per head |
| output gate | `sigmoid(z)` | `z * sigmoid(z)` (SiLU) |
| conv bias | none | seeds the accumulator |
| input | pre-split `mixed_qkv`/`gate`/`beta` | packed `qkvz`/`ba`, split internally |

The head topology alone settles it: KDA's `lp = H*K`, `q_off = i_h*K`,
`v_off = 2*lp + i_h*V` offsets cannot express `VH = 2*KH`. A mode flag would
double an existing kernel's branch factor to host a different algorithm, so this
ships as a sibling instead. `fused_kda_decode` is not exported from
`gated_delta_net/__init__.py`, so no existing interface is perturbed.

## Modifications

New:
  * `aiter/ops/triton/_gluon_kernels/gfx950/gated_delta_net/fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py`                            
    — the Gluon kernels. Two decompositions behind one entry point:                                              
    * **batch < 128** — `_fused_decode` / `_fused_decode_tiled`. One eight-wave                                  
      workgroup owns a token/key-head group's convolution history and both FP32                                  
      value-head states, with prefetch and tiling to hide memory latency while                                   
      the machine is under-occupied.                                                                             
    * **batch >= 128** — `_decode_group`, which keeps the whole `[V, K]` state                                   
      tile in registers across both matrix-vector products. Above that threshold                                 
      the kernel is bandwidth-bound, where the latency-hiding machinery stops                                    
      paying and the simpler traffic pattern reaches a better fraction of peak.                                  
                                                                                                                 
    Selection is a **range check, not a shape table**, so every batch size is                                    
    covered.  
* `aiter/ops/triton/gated_delta_net/fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — public wrapper,
  shape/dtype validation and the support predicate.
* `op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — a pure-torch fp32
  reference plus correctness, pad-slot, bf16-only and determinism tests.
* `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — bandwidth and
  roofline sweep.

Modified:
* `aiter/ops/triton/gated_delta_net/__init__.py` — export the op and its
  predicate.

### What it fuses

1. unpack packed `projected_qkvz` -> Q/K/V/Z and `projected_ba` -> b/a
2. depthwise causal conv1d against the rolling window, **with bias**, + SiLU
3. delta-rule gating, `decay = exp(-exp(A_log) * softplus(a + dt_bias))`
4. FP32 recurrent state update at `ssm_state[indices]`
5. gated RMSNorm with a SiLU gate
6. *optional* per-head group-128 FP8 quantization

Stage 6 is opt-in via `quant_dtype=`. With `None` the op returns bf16 only,
because an unquantized `Linear` consumer cannot accept an `(fp8, scales)` tuple.

### `pad_slot_id`

Rows whose state index equals `pad_slot_id` (default `-1`) are skipped without
reading or writing state. This matches what the other indexed-state ops in this
directory already do — `fused_conv_recurrent_norm` returns on `state_idx < 0`,
`causal_conv1d_update_split_qkv` takes an explicit `pad_slot_id` — and it is the
contract SGLang's `replay_state_indices_validator` documents. Measured cost:
**0.2-0.3%**, i.e. within noise.

## Scope and supported shapes

Deliberately narrow, and **reported rather than asserted**:
`fused_gdn_decode_qkvz_supported()` returns `(bool, reason)` so callers fall
back and can log why.

* gfx950 only — CDNA buffer addressing, `v_exp_f32`/`v_rcp_f32` inline asm,
  explicit register layouts
* `num_v_heads == 2 * num_k_heads`; `head_k_dim == head_v_dim == 128`
* conv width 4; contiguous conv and recurrent state pools
* bf16 packed projections / conv weight / conv bias / `dt_bias` / `norm_weight`;
  fp32 `A_log` and `ssm_state`; int32 state indices
* fp8 output, when requested, is `e4m3fn` or `e4m3fnuz`

**No CUDA path is affected.** The op is reachable only through its own module,
and every caller is expected to gate on the predicate.

## Accuracy Tests

`pytest op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py` — **22 passed** on
MI355X / ROCm 7.0 / Triton 3.8.

* `test_fused_gdn_decode_correctness` at batch 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 —
  output, scales, and both mutated state pools against the fp32 reference at
  ATOL/RTOL 0.05, the bar this directory already uses for `fused_kda_decode`.
* `test_fused_gdn_decode_pad_slot` — `PAD_SLOT_ID` rows leave `ssm_state` and
  `conv_state` bit-unchanged.
* `test_fused_gdn_decode_bf16_only` — `quant_dtype=None` returns `(out, None, None)`.
* `test_fused_gdn_decode_determinism` — same inputs twice, bit-identical.
* Eleven reference-only tests pin the packed layout, gate algebra and quant
  round-trip independently of the kernel.

The reference itself was validated before being trusted: run against **seven
independent implementations of this kernel across nine batch sizes**, it agrees
on every one, and `conv_state` matches **bit-exactly** on all 63 combinations.

## Speed Tests and Profiling

Hardware: 4x AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950), TP4 / EP1.
Image: `lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910` (ROCm 7.0,
Triton 3.8.0, torch 2.9). Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8`.

### Kernel level

Per-launch time under **CUDA graph replay** with a fixed 512-slot state pool.
Both matter: timing the Python call instead of the kernel produces a flat ~25 us
floor that is host overhead, and sizing the pool to the batch puts small batches
entirely in cache.

  | batch | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 | 192 | 256 |                                                     
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|                                                                  
  | this op (us/call) | 9.70 | 9.73 | 9.80 | 10.02 | 9.84 | 10.40 | 14.24 | 26.95 | 36.81 | 46.52 | 

Replaced chain, same conditions, per decode step over 36 GDN layers:
**830.8 us -> 279.2 us (2.98x)** for the four kernels listed in Motivation.

### Roofline

`python3 op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py`, MI355X
(8.0 TB/s peak HBM). The op performs no MFMA and no `gl.dot`; it is bound by the
FP32 recurrent state, read and written once per token per value head, which
dominates every other tensor by an order of magnitude.

  | batch | 1 | 8 | 32 | 64 | 128 | 192 | 256 |                                                                  
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|                                                                              
  | us/call | 9.39 | 9.69 | 10.40 | 14.24 | 26.95 | 36.81 | 46.52 |                                              
  | TB/s | 0.12 | 0.89 | 3.33 | 4.87 | 5.14 | 5.65 | **5.96** |
  | % peak | 1.4% | 11.2% | 41.6% | 60.8% | 64.3% | 70.6% | **74.5%** |

  Two regimes, and they are why the op carries two decompositions. Up to batch
  ~32 it is **latency-bound** — there is not enough state traffic to fill the
  machine, and time is nearly flat at ~9.4-10.4 us regardless of batch, so
  prefetch and tiling pay. From batch 64 it becomes **bandwidth-bound**, where
  that machinery stops paying and the register-resident tile reaches a better
  fraction of peak: **74.5% at batch 256**.

  A single decomposition plateaued at 5.20 TB/s (65%) there. Three candidate fixes
  were tested and rejected before concluding the gap was structural: extra HBM
  passes (identical byte counts, by source-level count of the state load/stores),
  launch-order locality (rewriting the grid to the other kernel's order gained
  0.75%), and store cache policy (`.cs` to `.wt`, slightly worse). What remains is
  the register layout and reduction structure — a different algorithm, not a
  tuning constant. 

### End to end (companion SGLang PR)

Un-profiled, random dataset ISL/OSL 1024/1024, `num-prompts == max-concurrency`.

| conc | baseline tok/s | with this op | delta | baseline TPOT | with op TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 459.9 | 487.4 | **+6.0%** | 4.27 ms | 4.03 ms |
| 8 | 3072.1 | 3262.3 | **+6.2%** | 5.07 ms | 4.76 ms |
| 32 | 8858.2 | 9666.3 | **+9.1%** | 6.86 ms | 6.26 ms |
| 64 | 13974.7 | 15109.6 | **+8.1%** | 8.60 ms | 7.91 ms |

GSM8K 1319q: 0.941 baseline vs 0.941 with the op, `Invalid: 0.000` on both.

  ### End to end at a raised graph cap

  The large-batch band only fires above batch 128, which requires
  `--cuda-graph-max-bs-decode` above its default of 64. At a cap of 256, two arms
  on the same base, un-profiled:                         

  | conc | baseline tok/s | with this op | delta | baseline TPOT | with op TPOT |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|                              
  | 128 | 21528.0 | 22596.2 | **+5.0%** | 11.00 ms | 10.43 ms |
  | 256 | 30926.3 | 32276.3 | **+4.4%** | 14.97 ms | 14.29 ms |

## Reproduction

```bash
docker run --rm -it --device /dev/kfd --device /dev/dri --network host \
  --group-add video --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  -v $HF_HOME:/hf lmsysorg/sglang-rocm:v0.5.19-rocm700-mi35x-20260910

pytest op_tests/triton_tests/test_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py -q
```

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added, mirroring the op tree (`op_tests/triton_tests/`)
- [x] `black` / `ruff` clean
- [x] DCO sign-off on every commit
- [x] gfx950-gated; no CUDA path affected
- [x] Benchmark (`op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_fused_gdn_decode_qkvz.py`)

## Motivation

Follow-up to #5350 (A4W4 CSV for `gemm_a4w4`). Qwen3.8-27B MXFP4 GDN `in_proj_ba` is dispatched through AITER Triton `gemm_afp4wfp4`. Those kernels load `GEMM-AFP4WFP4-N=<N>-K=<K>.json` by shape. gfx950 currently has no tiles for this model's BA widths.

On TP2, `in_proj_ba` scale rows are not divisible by 32, so vLLM always falls back to Triton for this layer. A TP2 A/B on MI355X (ISL 8192 / OSL 1024 / c=4) measured **+1.7% output tok/s** with the N=48 JSON vs `DEFAULT.json` (434.91 vs 427.68 tok/s). TP1 N=96 is scale-swizzle legal and stays on ASM unless a per-layer Triton force is applied, so that JSON is for the fallback / correctness path, not the default ASM path.

title: [Triton/Gluon] unified_attention: split the straggler generation of the 2-D prefill launch (KR_TAILSPLIT, gfx950)
body:
## What

For the 2-D prefill launch of `kernel_unified_attention_2d`, TTFT at moderate query counts is a step function of the workgroup count: ~2048 workgroups are co-resident on a 256-CU gfx950 (8/CU at the BLOCK_M=128 / 4-warp prefill config), and everything past a whole multiple runs as a nearly empty extra generation whose stragglers are latency-bound — a flat ~1.6 ms per layer regardless of how little work they carry. Measured on MI355X (GQA 8, head_dim 64, 61k paged KV, sinks): extend 4094 → 6.59 ms/layer; extend 4098 → 8.28 ms/layer (+26% for 4 tokens).

This adds a planner (default off, `KR_TAILSPLIT=1`) that runs the first whole multiple of the co-residency capacity through the **unmodified** kernel and splits only the thin remainder across KV segments (`kernel_unified_attention_2d_split` + `reduce_segments_tail`, sinks carried by segment 0). Sliding-window, all-decode, multi-seq, alibi/softcap, shuffled/uint8-KV shapes, and near-full tails (`MIN_SEG` guard) fall back bit-for-bit to the existing path. One subtlety worth reviewers' attention: the planner sizes the grid from `cdiv(max_seqlen_q, BLOCK_Q)`, not `q.shape[0]`, because callers that pad the token buffer (e.g. CUDA-graph capture buckets) otherwise inflate the plan with do-nothing blocks.

## Measured (MI355X gfx950, gpt-oss-120b, 4k-token extends over 61k cached KV)

- Boundary step 4094→4098: 25.5% → **0.08%**.
- Serving cc1 (sglang, 200 prompts): TTFT mean −6.1%, median −9.3%, P99 −8.7%; the bimodal TTFT distribution collapses (mean == median). At cc2 in the full config stack: −8–9%.
- Numerics: max_abs 1.22e-4 at the boundary shape, exactly 0.0 wherever the fallback engages; end-to-end gsm8k paired delta +0.015 (n=200).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: [Triton/Gluon] unified_attention: restructure the 2-D prefill tile loop — unmasked bulk + masked tail unlocks pipelining (−12.8% kernel, gfx950, default off)
body:
## What

The 2-D prefill kernel is VALU-issue-bound in its softmax epilogue, not memory-bound: co-resident programs march through KV tiles in lockstep, so the instantaneous KV working set is ~128 KB, per-XCD L2 traffic is far under capacity, and compulsory HBM traffic is ~23 GB/s — while the masked softmax path costs ~11.5 VALU slot-equivalents per score element, putting the stock kernel at ~74% of its own VALU roofline.

The stock tile body masks *every* score tile, which keeps the compiler from software-pipelining the loop. This restructures it: the tile body becomes a `MASKED: tl.constexpr` device helper (`_attention_tile`) called from two loops — an unmasked bulk pass over the tiles that lie strictly below the causal diagonal of every row in the q-block, and a masked tail pass for the rest. Removing the data-dependent masking from the bulk loop is what finally lets a deeper pipeline pay; `num_stages=2` is a measured null on the unmodified body, which is why the published `Q_GEQ_256` entry keeps it at 1.

Default off. Selected by `AITER_TRITON_UNIFIED_ATTN_FASTTILE`, or programmatically by `unified_attention_set_fasttile()`:

| value | schedule |
|---|---|
| `off` (default) | stock tile loop |
| `nofuse` | restructured loop, separate qk-scale multiply |
| `on` | restructured loop, `qk_scale` folded into the exp2 FMA |

**Gating.** The schedule was measured and certified on gfx950 prefill and nowhere else, so `_fasttile_modes()` declines every other architecture. It also declines all-decode (one query row, no bulk to speak of) and sliding-window layers — the bulk pass drops the window bound along with the causal one, so a gate that let a windowed layer through would be silently wrong rather than merely uncertified. There is a unit test for each of those four combinations, and a `tl.static_assert` in the helper catches a future mis-gating at compile time.

## Numerics

Neither active mode is bitwise identical to stock: the bulk/tail split reassociates the softmax epilogue, and the fold moves a rounding point (it replaces `(qk_scale * S) - m_j`, two roundings, with a single FMA).

But the arithmetic stays at the same width — fp32 accumulators, bf16 storage, same MFMA — so this **reassociates rather than truncates**. Scored against an fp64 reference at the production geometry (q=4094 / 61k KV, 16.8M elements):

```
        mean err            rms err             max err
stock   6.9682302246e-03    8.7645810784e-03    5.6726917642e-02
nofuse  6.9682298793e-03    8.7645804369e-03    5.6726917642e-02
on      6.9682298727e-03    8.7645804378e-03    5.6726917642e-02
```

99.72% of output elements are bitwise unchanged. Of the remainder, 23408 land **closer** to truth and 22894 land **farther** — a coin flip. Mean and RMS are unchanged to nine significant figures and the worst element is bit-identical across all three. The ~1.2e-4 max disagreement between modes is the gap between two equally-valid orderings, not an error term; both sit ~5.7e-2 from truth, and that distance is set by bf16 storage, which none of this touches.

Two things that aggregate view hides, stated plainly because they sound worse than they are:

- **Elementwise, some outputs move a lot in relative terms** — up to ~1.1e5 ULPs of their own magnitude. Every such element is near zero (the worst is at `|out|` = 3.6e-9, where the absolute error is 1.6e-6): a softmax-weighted sum of V that cancelled down to ~0 retains no significant digits, so one ULP moved upstream relocates it arbitrarily in relative terms. At p99.99 the elementwise drift is ≤3.3 ULPs. This is why the tests use a mixed rel/abs tolerance rather than a pure relative one — a pure relative bound is untestable on cancellation residue, and a pure absolute bound derived from `max|out|` lets small elements hide real errors.
- **Measured on random N(0,1) data.** The specific element counts won't transfer to real activations, though the mechanism doesn't depend on the distribution.

FP8 (`e4m3` q + KV) is covered by the same tests and is *better* behaved than bf16 — 1.1–1.7 max elementwise ULPs on three of the four shapes. The nvfp4 path was not decomposed this way.

## Measured (MI350X gfx950, 1 GPU, GQA 8, head_dim 64, sinks; ms/layer)

| shape | stock | nofuse | on |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4094 tokens / 61k KV | 7.372 | 6.545 (−11.2%) | 6.431 (−12.8%) |

Single-GPU microbenchmark on MI350X. End-to-end serving impact is not measured here.

## Tests

`op_tests/triton_tests/attention/test_unified_attention.py` gains 33 cases across four shapes, including one (`ragged`) whose `(567, 275)` entry carries more query tokens than cached keys — a shape that makes `context_len` negative and is what a `bulk_end` not clamped up to `tile_start` gets wrong.

Two things the tests do deliberately:

- **Every shape is checked against `use_2d_kernel` before it is trusted.** These schedules only touch the 2-D launch, and the suite's usual shapes route to the 3-D kernel, where a fasttile test would pass without executing a single restructured tile.
- **The comparison is against the stock kernel at a ULP budget, not against `ref_paged_attn` at the suite atol.** The bf16 floor is two orders of magnitude larger than the difference the restructure is allowed to introduce, so a torch-reference comparison alone would not catch a real bulk/tail-boundary bug. Measured drift is ≤0.62 bf16 ULP across all shapes; the tests fail at 2. Degenerate rows (no keys in range, no sink) are NaN in the stock kernel too, so the NaN pattern is required to match exactly.

Full suite on gfx950 passes identically in all three modes: 1121 passed, 0 failed.

title: [HIP] [JIT] Add optimized FlashKDA prefill kernels for gfx950
body:
## Motivation

This PR adds and optimizes a native HIP/MFMA FlashKDA prefill implementation for `gfx942` and `gfx950`.

The work is motivated by the following upstream integration changes:

- ATOM switched the Kimi K3 prefill path to aiter KDA:
  https://github.com/ROCm/ATOM/commit/16c20d3048ea4cf99d1cfc30fa8cbb01ffca12a9
- The aiter Triton KDA implementation was significantly improved:
  https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4683

After the Triton update, the original native HIP implementation was no longer competitive across the full K3 prefill workload range. This PR reworks the native preparation, recurrence, and output data flow to recover and extend the performance advantage on gfx950.

The primary optimization target is the public Kimi K3 TP8 prefill configuration:

```text
global heads = 96
tensor parallel size = 8
Hq = HV = 12 per rank
K = V = 128
```

The final gfx950 implementation was evaluated across:

- single-sequence prefill from 128 to 16K tokens;
- both fresh and resumed FP32 recurrent state at every tested length;
- uniform multi-sequence batches;
- ragged packed batches;
- multi-sequence resumed prefill;
- public zero-environment backend selection;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

Across the 20-cell prefill matrix and three random seeds, native HIP is faster than Triton in all 60 measured seed-cells. The geometric mean speedup is `1.403x`, with speedups ranging from `1.030x` to `1.830x`.

This PR additionally adds grouped value attention (GVA) as a functional extension of the native operator. GVA is not the primary performance claim of this PR.

Pure autoregressive decode is outside the scope of this PR. Kimi K3 decode continues to use its existing specialized fused recurrence kernel rather than `chunk_kimi_delta_attn`.

The native implementation is adapted from the HIP/MFMA backend of [MoonshotAI/FlashKDA](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA), source revision `7557ca0`, under the MIT license. The aiter integration, packed-sequence ABI, gfx950 optimizations, dispatch policies, and GVA extension are maintained in this PR.

## Technical Details

### Native operator integration

This PR adds an architecture-specialized FlashKDA forward implementation for `gfx942` and `gfx950` and integrates it with:

- aiter JIT compilation;
- architecture-specific source selection;
- the aiter tensor ABI and pybind layer;
- the public `chunk_kimi_delta_attn` interface;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

The native path supports the Kimi K3 prefill contract:

- BF16 Q, K, V, and raw gate inputs;
- FP32 or BF16 beta;
- FP32 `A_log` and `dt_bias`;
- `K = V = 128`;
- fused Q/K L2 normalization;
- fused gate processing;
- fused beta sigmoid;
- lower-bounded safe gate processing;
- V-first recurrent state;
- optional FP32/BF16 initial state;
- optional final-state output;
- dense and packed variable-length prefill;
- `int32` and `int64` packed sequence offsets at the Python boundary.

### Preparation fusion and data reuse

The native implementation uses two logical stages:

- K1 prepares the per-chunk operands required by the recurrence.
- K2 performs the recurrent scan and output calculation.

K1 fuses preparation work that would otherwise require multiple launches or repeated global-memory traffic, including:

- Q/K decay transformations;
- restored K operands;
- cumulative gate terms;
- beta activation;
- local inverse/Neumann terms;
- recurrence operands shared with K2.

K1 publishes these values in a layout selected for the corresponding K2 implementation. K2 reuses the prepared operands rather than reloading and recomputing them independently.

K1 and K2 remain separate physical kernels in the general path. The optimization is primarily fusion within K1 and producer/consumer reuse between K1 and K2, with selective fusion inside individual K2/output paths where the workload geometry makes it profitable.

### Shape-adaptive recurrence

The original plain C-split algorithm is retained as one valid route, but it is no longer used for every workload.

The gfx950 policy selects among several recurrence strategies:

- plain C-split;
- direct context processing;
- affine context scan;
- hybrid direct/scan processing;
- persistent and worklist-based variants.

The route is selected from sequence count, sequence length, packed geometry, recurrent-state mode, and the optional maximum-sequence-length hint.

The main algorithmic changes are:

- use a direct path when the recurrence can be completed efficiently without materializing a global scan structure;
- represent long-sequence chunks as affine state transformations so chunk-local producer work can run in parallel;
- restrict the serial scan to the compact cross-chunk state dependency;
- replay the chunk outputs in parallel after the scan;
- use hybrid routing for heterogeneous packed workloads;
- avoid unnecessary prefix construction on eligible paths;
- reuse activated beta, decay values, and recurrent operands between producer and replay stages;
- use persistent worklists to improve load balance for irregular packed inputs.

This keeps the inherently serial portion of the recurrence small while exposing preparation and output work to GPU parallelism.

### gfx950-specific implementation

The gfx950 implementation adds CDNA4-specific tuning, including:

- architecture-specific MFMA fragments and operand layouts;
- fused BT16 preparation;
- BT32 and BT64 merge paths;
- optimized register and LDS state exchange;
- multi-arena recurrence pipelines;
- packed-sequence prefix and worklist handling;
- direct global and K-split context paths;
- affine A/B producer and compact scan paths;
- persistent replay;
- specialized output replay paths;
- graph-stable, shape-based dispatch policies.

The resulting policy covers short launch-bound inputs, long low-batch inputs, large uniform batches, ragged packed inputs, and resumed prefill.

### Public backend routing

The public `chunk_kimi_delta_attn` wrapper supports:

- `backend="auto"`:
  use native HIP for supported calls on `gfx942`/`gfx950`, otherwise fall back to Triton;
- `backend="native"`:
  require native HIP and report an explicit rejection reason for unsupported inputs;
- `backend="triton"`:
  force the current Triton implementation;
- `backend="baseline"`:
  select the original Triton chunked implementation.

With no backend or KDA environment override, supported K3 prefill calls select native HIP automatically.

A host-provided `max_seqlen_upper_bound` is supported for packed inputs. This allows graph-safe route selection without copying device sequence metadata back to the host.

### Native ABI

The implementation provides validated raw-pointer entry points for the latency-sensitive dispatch path:

- raw v1 preserves the original equal-head interface;
- raw v2 appends the graph-safe maximum-sequence-length hint;
- raw v3 appends the Q/K head count required by GVA.

The v2 and v3 interfaces preserve the preceding ABI argument layout.

The adapter validates:

- tensor shapes and dtypes;
- dense and packed sequence geometry;
- recurrent-state layout;
- workspace capacity;
- GVA head ratios;
- active device;
- stream ownership;
- architecture support;
- graph-safe routing bounds.

### GVA functional support

The native operator additionally supports grouped value attention when:

```text
HV >= Hq
HV % Hq == 0
```

Value, gate, and state heads are mapped to Q/K heads using:

```text
qk_head = value_head // (HV / Hq)
```

The GVA implementation covers:

- ratio-2 and ratio-4 head mappings;
- dense and packed layouts;
- fresh and resumed prefill;
- optional final-state output;
- empty packed sequences;
- descriptor and raw-v3 equivalence;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

GVA is an operator-level compatibility feature. The primary performance results in this PR use the current public Kimi K3 equal-head geometry, `Hq=HV=12`.

### Test and benchmark integration

Correctness tests are integrated into the standard pytest hierarchy:

```text
op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native.py
op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native_python_api.py
```

Performance coverage is integrated into the standard benchmark hierarchy:

```text
op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_flash_kda_native.py
```

The benchmark compares public zero-environment HIP routing against the forced Triton path using identical inputs. It records:

- eager and ROCm graph correctness;
- output and final-state relative RMS;
- p10, p50, p90, mean, and standard deviation;
- raw paired timing samples;
- HIP win fraction;
- speedup over Triton;
- kernel route and graph topology;
- CSV and JSON artifacts.

A thin reproducibility runner is provided at:

```text
scripts/run_flash_kda_gva_acceptance.sh
```

The runner delegates correctness and performance validation to the canonical pytest and benchmark files. It also uses an isolated JIT directory and records the tested Git revision, environment, logs, benchmark output, and native module checksum.

## Test Plan

### Correctness

Run the standard Python API and native GPU tests:

```bash
python -m pytest -q \
  op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native_python_api.py \
  op_tests/triton_tests/chunk_delta_attn/test_flash_kda_native.py
```

The tests cover:

- public API validation;
- native admission and fallback behavior;
- raw v1/v2/v3 dispatch;
- dense and packed variable-length prefill;
- fresh and resumed recurrent state;
- equal-head attention;
- GVA ratio-2 and ratio-4 mappings;
- empty packed sequences;
- native versus Triton numerical agreement;
- native versus FP32 recurrence reference;
- descriptor versus raw-v3 equivalence;
- public automatic routing;
- ROCm graph capture and replay.

### Primary equal-head performance matrix

The primary performance comparison uses the public K3 TP8 configuration:

```text
Hq = HV = 12
K = V = 128
state = None or FP32 [N, 12, 128, 128]
execution = ROCm graph replay
```

The following single-sequence lengths are crossed with both state modes:

```text
128, 256, 512, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K
```

State modes:

```text
fresh:   initial_state=None
resume:  nonzero FP32 initial_state
```

Additional packed coverage:

```text
batch-16x1K fresh
batch-64x256 fresh
ragged-16K fresh
resume-4x4K FP32
```

The formal comparison uses:

```text
backends:                    public zero-env HIP vs forced Triton
seeds:                       42, 43, 44
warmup:                      20 iterations
measurements:                120 per backend/cell/seed
execution:                   ROCm graph replay
measurement order:           alternating and position-balanced
paired bootstrap resamples:  10,000
relative-RMS tolerance:       0.04
```

A performance cell passes only when:

1. HIP p50 is faster than Triton for every seed.
2. The paired HIP win fraction is greater than 50% for every seed.
3. The upper bound of every per-seed paired-p50 95% bootstrap confidence interval is below zero.
4. The upper bound of the cross-seed paired-p50 95% bootstrap confidence interval is below zero.

The regular benchmark entry point can be used for reproduction:

```bash
python op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/bench_flash_kda_native.py \
  --suite core \
  --heads 12 \
  --value-heads 12 \
  --backend native \
  --backend triton \
  --execution graph \
  --public-k3 \
  --warmup 20 \
  --repeat 120 \
  --seed 42 \
  --tolerance 0.04 \
  --require-arch gfx950 \
  --require-compute-units 256
```

The same benchmark is repeated for seeds `43` and `44`, and for each single sequence length with a nonzero FP32 initial state.

### GVA functional coverage

GVA is validated separately with:

```text
Hq=2, HV=4
Hq=2, HV=8
```

The GVA tests verify numerical correctness, state layout, public routing, raw-v3 dispatch, packed metadata, and graph replay. GVA performance is not used as the primary performance claim of this PR.

## Test Result

Test environment:

```text
Host:      smci355-ccs-aus-n12-25.cs-aus.dcgpu
GPU:       MI355X / gfx950, 256 compute units
PyTorch:   2.10.0+rocm7.2.4.git3d3aa833
ROCm:      7.2.53211
Execution: ROCm graph replay
```

### Correctness

```text
81 passed in 578.35s
```

For the primary equal-head performance matrix:

```text
logical cells:              20
seeds per cell:             3
total measured seed-cells:  60
p50 wins:                   60 / 60
speedup range:              1.030x - 1.830x
speedup geometric mean:     1.403x
```

All per-seed and cross-seed paired-p50 bootstrap confidence intervals have an upper bound below zero.

The weakest cell is `single-512-fresh`:

```text
worst-seed speedup:          1.030x
worst-seed HIP win fraction: 70.8%
pooled paired p50 delta:     -1.839 us
95% confidence interval:     [-2.620, -0.920] us
```

Even for this launch-bound case, the upper confidence bound remains below zero.

Speedup is defined as:

```text
speedup = Triton p50 / native HIP p50
```

For the following tables, latency is the median of the three per-seed p50 measurements. “Worst speedup” is the minimum speedup observed across seeds 42, 43, and 44.

### Single-sequence fresh/resume cross coverage

| Length | HIP fresh p50 | Triton fresh p50 | Worst fresh speedup | HIP resume p50 | Triton resume p50 | Worst resume speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 128 | 31.201 us | 34.600 us | 1.103x | 31.840 us | 38.481 us | 1.206x |
| 256 | 34.260 us | 40.720 us | 1.182x | 34.580 us | 45.881 us | 1.323x |
| 512 | 49.740 us | 51.360 us | 1.030x | 49.640 us | 56.760 us | 1.134x |
| 1K | 66.960 us | 78.180 us | 1.163x | 67.461 us | 82.601 us | 1.216x |
| 2K | 85.881 us | 118.641 us | 1.376x | 86.001 us | 122.641 us | 1.424x |
| 4K | 117.841 us | 208.382 us | 1.765x | 118.981 us | 212.242 us | 1.783x |
| 8K | 208.462 us | 352.583 us | 1.691x | 205.982 us | 354.543 us | 1.719x |
| 16K | 368.483 us | 621.285 us | 1.684x | 366.123 us | 620.106 us | 1.693x |

Subgroup geometric means across all three seeds:

| State | Seed-cells | Geometric-mean speedup | Minimum speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Fresh single sequence | 24 | 1.350x | 1.030x |
| Resumed single sequence | 24 | 1.421x | 1.134x |

### Batched and ragged prefill coverage

| Workload | HIP p50 | Triton p50 | Worst speedup | Worst HIP win rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| batch-16x1K fresh | 183.582 us | 333.543 us | 1.812x | 100% |
| batch-64x256 fresh | 189.382 us | 323.683 us | 1.708x | 100% |
| ragged-16K fresh | 366.143 us | 461.124 us | 1.256x | 100% |
| resume-4x4K FP32 | 335.363 us | 409.324 us | 1.216x | 100% |

The four batched/ragged cases have a combined geometric-mean speedup of `1.478x`, with a minimum speedup of `1.216x`.

### Numerical and graph validation

Across the 60 primary performance seed-cells:

```text
maximum output relative RMS:      4.936e-3
maximum final-state relative RMS: 4.207e-3
configured tolerance:             4.000e-2
```

The following contract checks also passed:

- public zero-environment routing selected native HIP;
- public routing was storage-bitwise identical to explicit native routing;
- eager and graph-replay output were storage-bitwise identical;
- eager and graph-replay final state were storage-bitwise identical;
- input initial state remained unchanged;
- output and final-state dtype contracts were preserved;
- expected native and Triton graph routes were observed.

### GVA result

GVA functional coverage passed for ratio-2 and ratio-4 configurations, including dense/packed layouts, fresh/resumed state, raw-v3 dispatch, and graph replay.

These GVA results establish functional support only. The primary performance claim remains the equal-head Kimi K3 TP8 prefill matrix above.

Runtime performance reported in this PR was measured on gfx950. The gfx942 implementation is included, but gfx942 runtime performance is not part of this result set.

## Submission Checklist

- [ ] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.
```
