title: [JIT] Identify MI350P, and stop hardcoding the XCD count
body:
## Motivation

1. **`get_device_name()` misreports MI308 as MI300 on ROCm 7.1 and newer.**
   `_get_pci_chip_id` hardcoded `hipDeviceAttributePciChipId = 10019`, but 7.1 inserted
   `MaxAvailableVgprsPerThread` ahead of it and renumbered everything after. The call still
   succeeds and still returns an integer, so the result is tested against `MI308_CHIP_IDS`
   and silently misses.

2. **MI350P was not identified at all.** It is a half-size gfx950 (4 XCDs against 8 on
   MI350X/MI355X), and `get_device_name()` returned `"MI350"` for it.

3. **The XCD count was hardcoded to 8**, with a comment saying it could not be queried. It
   can, from ROCm 7.0 on. On a 4-XCD part every `remap_xcd` consumer computes its L2
   locality swizzle against the wrong die count.

## Test Result

Three parts, all HIP 7.2. Top four rows are raw HIP and sysfs reads, bottom three are what
aiter's shipped functions return:

| | MI300X (gfx942) | MI350P (gfx950) | MI355X (gfx950) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| raw `NumberOfXccs` (10018) | 8 | **4** | 8 |
| raw `PciChipId` old (10019) | 512 | 512 | 512 |
| raw `PciChipId` new (10020) | `0x74A1` | `0x75A8` | `0x75A3` |
| sysfs device id | `0x74A1` | `0x75A8` | `0x75A3` |
| `get_num_xcds()` | 8 | **4** | 8 |
| `_get_pci_chip_id()` | `0x74A1` | `0x75A8` | `0x75A3` |
| `get_device_name()` | `MI300` | **`MI350P`** | `MI350` |

`10019` returns 512 on every part because it is `MaxAvailableVgprsPerThread`, not a chip id.
`10020` matches sysfs everywhere. MI355X is the negative control for the new name: same
architecture as MI350P, 8 dies rather than 4, so it stays `MI350`.

Reproducible with a ctypes read of attributes 10018/10019/10020 cross-checked against
`/sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/device`.

**On MI308 this is inference, not observation**. `10019` returned 512 on all
three parts above, `MaxAvailableVgprsPerThread` is an architectural constant, and MI308 is
gfx942 like the MI300X measured, so it returns 512 there too and 512 is not in
`MI308_CHIP_IDS = {0x74A2, 0x74A8, 0x74B6, 0x74BC}`. Untested: a ROCm < 7.1 box, where the
guard should still select 10019.

## Notes

**Why the die count and not the chip id.** MI350P reports `0x75A8`, which hipBLASLt's
Tensile table lists as [`mi350-unknown1`](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-libraries/blob/develop/projects/hipblaslt/tensilelite/include/Tensile/AMDGPUPredicates.hpp#L69), alongside a sibling `0x75B8`. 
So it's unclear those ids can be considered stable enough.

**What the die count does not distinguish.** Compute partitioning (SPX/DPX/TPX/CPX) means a
partition sees a subset of the dies, so a DPX-partitioned MI350X would also report 4 XCCs
and be named `MI350P`. That may be wanted, but it deserves a comment either way.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Add fused Qwen3-Next GDN prefill (gfx950 Gluon) with fp8 group-quant epilogue
body:
A single fused op for the Qwen3-Next gated delta-net *prefill* chain (causal_conv1d_split_qkv -> fused gating -> fp32 chunked delta scan -> gated RMSNorm -> per-head group-128 FP8 quant), replacing the four-kernel path with a tight set of Gluon launches that fuse the work intra-kernel and drop the intermediate HBM traffic. The FP8 activations a block-FP8 out_proj consumes are emitted by the epilogue launch (no separate quant kernel).

Support is reported, not asserted: fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz_supported gates on gfx950, Triton >= 3.8 (Gluon dialect), and an in-range (tokens, batch)/dtype contract, so callers fall back to the four-kernel chain instead of crashing. Prefill spans a wide token range, so it dispatches one of four autotuned M-tile schedules. The Gluon/HIP tiles import lazily on dispatch, keeping the module and the support predicate importable on any platform.

Tests: pure-torch fp32 sequential-scan reference (deliberately not the chunked algorithm) at the kernel's bf16 rounding boundaries; 9/9 pass on MI355X (gfx950, Triton 3.8). Includes an op benchmark.

### Motivation
  The Qwen3-Next GDN (gated delta-net) **prefill** is a four-kernel chain today:
  `causal_conv1d_split_qkv` → fused gating → the fp32 chunked delta-rule scan →
  gated RMSNorm + per-head group-128 FP8 quant. Four launches means the large
  intermediate tensors (split qkv, conv output, gated core) round-trip through HBM
  between every step.

  This PR adds a single fused Gluon op, `fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz`, that folds that
  work intra-kernel: split + conv + SiLU + QK-norm + gating-prep in one launch, the
  fp32 chunked scan, and a gated-RMSNorm + group-128 FP8-quant **epilogue**. The win
  is the intra-launch fusion and the dropped intermediate HBM traffic. The FP8
  activations a block-FP8 `out_proj` consumes are emitted by the epilogue launch, so
  there is no separate quantization kernel.

  This is the **prefill sibling of the decode kernel** (ROCm/aiter#5520): same
  Qwen3-Next GDN math, but it consumes ragged variable-length batches
  (`cu_seqlens` + `has_initial_state`) and runs the fp32 chunked scan instead of the
  single-token recurrent update.

  ### Design
  - **Reported, not asserted.** `fused_gdn_prefill_qkvz_supported(...) -> (bool, reason)`
    gates on **gfx950** (CDNA buffer addressing / inline asm / explicit register
    layouts) and **Triton ≥ 3.8** (the tiles are the Gluon dialect; some ROCm 3.7
    builds import `triton.experimental.gluon` but fail to compile it, so the gate is a
    version check, not just an import probe). Callers fall back to the four-kernel
    chain instead of crashing.
  - **Lazy tile import** on the dispatch path, so the module and the support predicate
    stay importable on any platform (older Triton, non-gfx950, CUDA).
  - Prefill spans a wide token range, so it dispatches one of **four autotuned M-tile

      projected_qkvz, projected_ba, conv_state, delta_state,

title: [Triton/Gluon] [HIP] [JIT] Add Windows support
body:
## Motivation

aiter has no Windows support: `__init__.py` force-enables `AITER_TRITON_ONLY` on `win32`, and the JIT layer assumes Linux-only tooling (`rocminfo`, `libamdhip64.so`, `/dev/null`, `rm -rf`, ELF linker flags). This wires the JIT and Python layers up to the Windows ROCm stack so CK- and HIP-based ops compile and run there.

## Technical Details

Toolchain discovery - ROCm tools ship as `.exe`/`.bat` wrappers on Windows, so executable lookup goes through a suffix-aware `_find_executable`, and `_find_rocm_home` falls back to `HIP_PATH`. `get_cxx_compiler` returns hipcc, the only compiler on Windows that can build both the .cpp and .hip sources.

GPU info - `chip_info` uses `hipinfo` in place of `rocminfo`, with a parser per output format, and loads the version-suffixed `amdhip64*.dll`. `--offload-arch=native` shells out to offload-arch, which cannot detect the GPU on Windows, so `native` resolves via `_detect_native()` instead.

Build system - ELF/GNU-ld-only flags (`-fPIC`, `-mcmodel=large`, `--gc-sections`, `-fvisibility=*`, `_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI`) are excluded on Windows; `_ninja_path` escapes drive-letter colons, which ninja otherwise reads as rule separators; PE links against `pythonXYZ.lib`; `-D_USE_MATH_DEFINES` is added since the UCRT only declares `M_SQRT2` & friends under it. `compile_lib` drives hipcc with ninja instead of make.

Stale-lock fix - `FileBaton._pid_alive` no longer probes with `os.kill(pid, 0)` on Windows: CPython maps that onto `TerminateProcess`, so the liveness check would kill the very builder it was checking on.

Several shell idioms are also replaced with portable equivalents that are more robust on Linux too: `os.system("rm -rf")`, `os.popen("cat /proc/sys/kernel/numa_balancing")`, `echo ... | hipcc -`, and the shelled-out `hipcc` and `hipconfig` calls in `csrc/cpp_itfs/utils.py`.

`check_LLVM_MAIN_REVISION` needed more than the shell change. Its probe relies on CTAD, and at hipcc's default standard on Windows it failed on a template-argument error rather than on the `__host__ __device__` rule it is meant to measure, so the function returned the same value whatever the toolchain did. The probe is now pinned to `-std=c++20`, the standard the modules are built with. On Linux clang already defaults to `gnu++17`, so the answer there is unchanged.

`arch_info.get_arch()` now probes Triton on first call instead of at import. Since #5590 the flash-attention Triton backend imports `tuned_config_utils`, which imports `arch_info`, so importing it on a host with no GPU driver raised and then fell through to the `jax` fallback. This is what fails the Windows Smoke Test on `main`.

## Test Plan

Windows 11, RDNA4, TheRock ROCm 7, Python 3.12. Each op runs in its own subprocess against a torch reference, both from the repo and from a `pip install .`'d wheel.

## Test Result

| Op | Result |
|---|---|
| `rms_norm` | OK |
| `rmsnorm2d_fwd` | OK |
| `silu_and_mul` | OK |
| `topk_softmax` | OK |
| `rotary_embedding_fwd` | OK |

`import aiter` builds and loads the full CK/HIP path - previously Windows exited before any op was loaded.

Not covered: ops whose modules run a CK-tile blob generator (layernorm2d, the CK GEMMs, flash-attn). Those generators emit hundreds of specializations and dominate build time on Linux equally, so this is not a Windows-specific gap, but that path is untested here.

## Submission Checklist

- [x] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.

title: [FlyDSL] One stage and two-stage ring all-reduce kernels for PCIe interconnects
body:
## Motivation

PR #4970 introduced a two-stage int4 quick reduce FlyDS kernel that improved all-reduce throughput over the existing Aiter two-stage/RCCL kernels. Current Aiter all-reduce kernels are written primarily for the xGMI interconnect. This PR optimizes the FlyDSL quick reduce int4 kernel for PCIe interconnects (MI350P) and adds two new kernels: a one-stage lossless and a two-stage ring kernel with int4/int6 codecs. On MI350P, they offer better performance than the existing Aiter production kernels (RCCL/cross-device-reduce)

Category | Speedup TP=2 | Speedup TP=4 | Speedup TP=8
-- | -- | -- | --
Decode (new kernels are exact) | 1.40x-2.27x (avg: 1.62x) | 1.45x-5.60x (avg: 2.25x) | 2.36x-4.60x (avg: 3.18x)
Prefill (new kernels use quantization) | 2.42x-3.54x (avg: 2.94x) | 2.50x-3.89x (avg: 3.08x) | 2.43x-4.84x (avg: 3.57x)

## Technical Details

**Kernels** (`aiter/ops/flydsl/kernels/`)
- `one_shot_allreduce.py`: exact one-stage push all-reduce. bf16 in and out, fp32 accumulation in a fixed rank order. The IPC inbox is double-buffered by color parity.
- `quick_allreduce_int4_ring.py`: two-stage ring schedule, 2(N-1) single-destination hops, with a wire format (int4/int6) chosen separately for each lap. At TP8 the reduce-scatter lap defaults to INT6 so the ring holds the 18 dB SQNR floor.
- `quick_allreduce_codec.py` and `quick_allreduce_shared.py`: the INT4, INT6 and fp16 wire formats and the transport shared by the mesh and ring schedules. The #4970 mesh kernel is refactored onto them.

**Host wrappers** (`aiter/ops/flydsl/`)
- `QuickAllReduceInt4` gains an `algorithm="mesh"|"ring"` choice, per-lap codecs, inbox memory modes, and payload-size super-tile ladders.
- `OneShotAllReduce` is a new host wrapper for the one-stage kernel. It picks a per-fabric rung (`ONESHOT_LADDER`) by payload size.
- Fabric detection (`has_xgmi_peer_links`) reads KFD link types. PCIe hosts get a fine-grained inbox, because uncached peer writes serialize per destination on PCIe. On xGMI we use un-cached IPC memory.

**Production dispatch**, opt-in with `AITER_FLY_AR=1` - the existing behavior is unchanged when the env variable is unset/disabled.
- The custom-all-reduce slot is fronted by the exact one-shot for plain bf16 up to the policy ceiling.
- The quick-reduce slot, under `AITER_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4`, dispatches bf16 payloads in the policy window to the FlyDSL mesh or ring instance.
- The windows come from `allreduce_policy.FAMILY_POLICY`, keyed on (fabric, world size). They can be overridden with `AITER_FLY_AR_ONESHOT_MAX_BYTES` and `AITER_FLY_AR_MESH_MAX_BYTES`.
- `CudaCommunicator.destroy()` now closes the all-reduce slots it owns. That releases the IPC handles before the process group goes away.
- Fabric detection is per host. The assumption that a node is uniformly either xGMI or PCIe.

## Test Plan

Added option to use fp16 codec over the wire. This ensures lossless transport and allows to verify the transport correctness using a bitwise equality/all close against a reference implementation. The new one-stage kernel is exact by construction. Added/modified the following test suites that run under the CI
-  `test_flydsl_quick_allreduce_int4.py`: Added tests for the ring algorithm, added transport correctness tests for both mesh and ring algorithm.
- `test_reuse_identical_rank_groups.py`: Added tests to ensure that `CudaCommunicator.destroy()` now closes the all-reduce slots it owns.
- `test_flydsl_one_shot_allreduce.py`: New test suite for the one-stage exact all-reduce kernel.

All tests should pass on CI to verify the code changes form this PR.

Created a separate benchmarking suite for communication collective under `op_tests/op_benchmarks/flydsl`
- `bench_comm_allreduce.py`: Comprehensive benchmarking suite for Aiter's all-reduce collectives. Can be extended to include the fused all-reduce variants.
- `transferbench_roofline.py`: Optional roofloine analysis using TransferBench. Used in the benchmarking script with additional `--roofline` flag to provide wire-efficiency estimate of the different all-reduce implementations.

The benchmarking suite is used to tune the instance selection as well to produce performance claims in this PR. The suite can be used to tune any all-reduce implementations, not just the FlyDSL ones.   ‎

## Test Result

<!-- Briefly summarize test outcomes. -->

title: [FlyDSL] Adaptive decode Top-K kernel, dispatched by one measured gate
body:
# Adaptive decode Top-K kernel, dispatched by one measured gate

The decode path now has four candidate kernels and no single one wins the shape space, so this adds the kernel behind a table of measured row intervals keyed by `(arch, CU count, emit, k, width)`. An `(arch, CU count)` pair the table does not name keeps today's behaviour exactly.

## How the dispatch works

Two public entry points reach the decode path, and they do not share a call chain: `topk_select()` routes its `decode` arm straight into the FlyDSL host and never passes through `top_k_per_row_decode()`. So the gate sits in both, and both ask one function rather than deciding for themselves, which is what keeps them from disagreeing about a shape.

```
  top_k_per_row_decode()              topk_select()
  aiter/ops/topk.py                   aiter/ops/topk_select.py
          |                              |- argmax / small_k / plain
          |                              |- stream
          |                              \- decode
          |                                   |
          |                                   v
          |                     flydsl_top_k_per_row_decode()
          |                     aiter/ops/flydsl/topk/topk_per_row.py
          |                                   |
    [gate here]                         [gate here]
          |                                   |
          +-----------------+-----------------+
                            v
              decode_backend_for_call()   <- the only decision
                            |
     +----------------------+---------------------+
     v                      v                     v
  adaptive               chunked              upstream
  (in a band of          (in upstream's       (not ours; the dispatch
   the measured           chunked gate,        below picks the port
   table, looked up       read at the          where enabled, else the
   at the live length)    physical width)      HIP/C++ kernel)
```

The gate never names the fallback kernel itself: it answers "not ours" and upstream's existing dispatch picks, which is the port on gfx950 and gfx1250 and the HIP/C++ kernel elsewhere. That is also why a caller wanting values never reaches the adaptive kernel, which emits indices only. Only `top_k_per_row_decode()` has that dispatch below it. In `topk_select()` the decode arm is already chosen, so "not ours" leaves the chunked kernel.

## `max_row_len`, and what a caller has to pass

A decode buffer is allocated once at the model's maximum context and a call fills whatever part of it the requests need. `seq_lens` is device-resident, so the host cannot read it without a sync, and the adaptive kernel picks its tier, part count and workspace on the host before launch. Given only the buffer, it builds a short row as if it were a full one.

So the new argument states the longest live row in the batch. A serving stack that assembles the batch already has it -- it is `max(seqLens)`. No caller in aiter passes it yet, so nothing reaches the new kernel until a stack opts in. The tables below declare it.

- **It is a guarantee, not a hint.** Part of what it selects is compiled in, so a bound below the longest live row returns wrong indices rather than merely slower ones. It cannot be checked here without the sync this path exists to avoid. A bound above it is always correct; it only costs the win.
- **`None` declines the adaptive kernel and nothing else.** The chunked bands keep reading the physical width they were fitted on, so a call that passes nothing routes exactly where it routes today.
- **It never changes a result**, only which kernel produces it.

## Results

Every cell is scored, not only the ones the gate takes. A band takes a cell when the kernel is no slower than the best of the four and at least 1.05x faster than what runs there today; a smaller margin is noise. Every entry had to satisfy that on **both** slices below, so a cell that only clears it on the diagonal is not in the table. Nothing is behind on either slice.

A ratio is today's kernel over this PR's, so a declined cell is 1.00x by construction and the geomean covers every cell. Each card's own grid and per-cell winners are below.

Protocol: all four arms are timed the same way on every cell, under graph replay, and the cell's number is the median over its repeats; cells where the arms came out close were re-timed with more.

**On the diagonal**, where the buffer is exactly full.

| device | cells | cells taken | geomean | worst cell | behind |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI308X, gfx942, 80 CU | 1000 | 433 | 1.34x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300A, gfx942, 228 CU | 1000 | 388 | 1.35x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300X, gfx942, 304 CU | 1000 | 361 | 1.32x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI355X, gfx950, 256 CU | 1000 | 311 | 1.13x | 1.00x | 0 |

**On padded buffers**, a 1048576 buffer holding a shorter live row with `max_row_len` set to that length, which is what production allocates and what a serving stack would pass. Same table, looked up at the bound.

| device | cells | cells taken | geomean | worst cell | behind |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MI308X, gfx942, 80 CU | 900 | 369 | 1.29x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300A, gfx942, 228 CU | 900 | 315 | 1.25x | 1.00x | 0 |
| MI300X, gfx942, 304 CU | 900 | 288 | 1.22x | 1.00x | 0 |

The bound is what makes the second table look like the first. One k per group, and cells too large to allocate in a unit test are skipped. Every cell runs twice, once on planted logits whose top k sit at known positions and once on random ones; ragged `seq_lens` with the longest row exactly on the bound get the same treatment.
- Across the sweeps above, every arm's output was checked against `torch.topk` over each row's live slice: 7600 cells over four cards, no incorrect result. On the 3600 padded cells everything past the live length held a poison value, so a read past `seq_lens` would have come back as a wrong answer rather than a plausible one.

- **Ragged batches are calibrated optimistically.** The gate decides once per call on the longest row, because the kernel is configured once per launch, and the sweeps hold uniform batches. A row that would win 1.31x on its own measures 0.66x when a much longer row shares its batch. Correctness is unaffected; the win is.
- **Reduce the reps with `min` instead of the median** and two entries show near-ties. 304 CU reads 3 losing cells, worst 0.98x, at k=512 and a live length of 8192; 256 CU reads 2, worst 0.997x, at width 131072 and 32 rows. All five clear the kernel their own card runs -- by 1.16x to 2.19x on 256 CU -- and lose to a third kernel by under 2%.
- **gfx1250 is unmeasured** and has no entry, so the gate declines it and it runs exactly what it runs today. gfx950 is measured at one CU count.
- **CI.** The routing test skips without a device, and the widest band edges are too large to allocate inside a unit test.
- **Indices only.** Emitting values is a kernel change, not proposed here.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Perf] Optimize live-window unified-attention decode
body:
## Summary

- Partition the 3-D unified-attention decode kernel over the live sliding window instead of the full logical sequence.
- Apply the same live-segment bound in the Triton and gfx1250 Gluon reducers.
- Select 3-D from decode state, active KV length, and available launch parallelism, independent of GPU architecture and head size.
- Cover a large, off-tile sliding window in the existing unified-attention regression suite; no standalone dispatcher-coupled test file is added.
- On gfx1250, use the existing Gluon 3-D producer for the affected unshuffled FP8 live-window path. This backend choice is separate from the architecture-agnostic 2-D/3-D workload selection.

## Motivation

For sliding-window decode, the previous 3-D kernel derived segment boundaries from the full sequence length. It could therefore visit expired KV tiles before masking them and leave leading reduction segments empty when the logical context was much longer than the active window.

This change rebases 3-D segment ranges onto the first tile intersecting the live window and makes each reducer consume only active live-window segments. It changes neither the attention mask nor the stored KV layout.

## Dispatch and platform scope

The 2-D/3-D selector now chooses 3-D only when all of the following are true:

- the batch is decode-only;
- the active KV length exceeds the existing 2-D short-context boundary;
- the 2-D launch does not already exceed the target launch parallelism.

Short windows, prefills, and already-parallel launches retain the previous 2-D route. There is no model name, product name, GPU-architecture gate, or head-size gate in this workload decision.

The existing architecture-specific kernel implementations and low-level launch tuning remain architecture-specific. In particular, gfx1250 already uses its Gluon 3-D producer for shuffled KV. The wrapper now also uses that available producer for unshuffled FP8 live-window 3-D decode, after gfx1250 testing showed non-finite partials in the generic Triton FP8 producer. No ASIC-revision or model-specific condition is introduced.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [PA] Support Q/K D192 with asymmetric K/V head dim
body:
## Motivation

<!-- Explain the purpose of this PR and the goals it aims to achieve. -->
Extend Gluon paged decode to support Q/K D192 with an independent V/output dimension in the one-KV-head persistent path. 
This enables `MiMo-v2.5-Pro` native physical Q/K192-V128 BF16 and FP8 page-64 caches without padding V to 192.
Existing symmetric Q/K/V configurations remain as the default. 

## Technical Details

<!-- Explain the changes along with any relevant GitHub links. -->

Gluon PA decode assumes equal Q/K and V/output dimensions, preventing native Q/K192-V128 caches. 
D192 also uses an internally padded D256 MFMA layout, so padded K/V and reduction accesses require bounds masks. Persistent execution must keep local split bounds separate from the global bottom-right causal frontier.

This PR extended PA gluon kernel with supported asymmetric scope: 
- gfx942 and gfx950;
- Q/K D192 and V/output D128;
- BF16 or FP8 KV cache;
- page size 64, vectorized-5D K/V layout;
- query length 1 decode and query length 4 target verification;
- full attention and sliding-window attention with learned sinks;
- one KV head;
- persistent PS or one-shot execution.

**Modifications:**
- Propagate independent `HEAD_SIZE` and `VALUE_HEAD_SIZE` through the host and one-KV-head persistent path: Q/K width drives QK, while V width drives PV, temporary buffers, output stores, and reduction.
- Infer and validate the physical K/V dimensions and allocate temporary output from the V/output width.
- Mask padded D192 K/V/reduction accesses and separate local split bounds from the global bottom-right causal frontier.
- Add PyTorch-reference tests for BF16/FP8 page-64 vectorized caches covering decode, MTP, full attention, SWA, and learned sinks.

## Test Plan

title: [Triton/Gluon] [FlyDSL] Fused K5 + K6 gfx942 kernel for linear attention prefill
body:
## Motivation

The gated-delta-rule (GDN / KDA) prefill pipeline runs as six stages, K1–K6. Two of them
dominate the tail: **K5**, the inter-chunk hidden-state scan, and **K6**, the inter/intra-chunk
output projection.

There is no fused K5+K6 kernel for `gfx942` today. The `gfx942` path runs K5 and K6 as two separate
kernels, which forces the entire K5→K6 handoff through HBM: the per-chunk `h` snapshots
(`BV·K` per chunk) and the gated `v_new` (`BT·BV` per chunk) are written out by K5 and
immediately read back by K6. On a kernel that is already memory-bound, that round-trip is the
single largest avoidable cost.

This PR adds that fused kernel, and in the process makes the standalone K5 kernel faster than
existing `gfx942` backends (Triton, HIP, FlyDSL) for most shapes measured. Both improvements are
independently useful: the fused kernel wins where the grid is large enough to fill the device,
and the improved standalone K5 carries the shapes where it is not.

Benchmarked 31 production shapes on MI325X and MI300X (Kimi-K3 KDA at TP8/TP4, Qwen3-Next GDN at TP8/TP4, Qwen3.5-MoE GDN at TP1/TP8, Qwen3 GDN at TP1):

**K5 standalone** — geomean speedup vs Triton (31 shapes):

| Kernel | vs Triton | vs HIP |
|---|---|---|
| FlyDSL (`flydsl_opt`, PR #4732) — unsafe conv | 1.86× | 1.08× |
| FlyDSL VK (this PR) — safe conv, shipped default | 1.96× | 1.15× |
| FlyDSL VK (this PR) — unsafe conv (`AITER_FAST_FP32_TO_FP16=1`) | 2.24× | 1.32× |

**K5+K6** — geomean speedup vs Triton K5+K6 (31 shapes, `fused_auto` routing):

| Kernel | vs Triton+Triton | vs HIP+Triton |
|---|---|---|
| `flydsl_opt`+Triton K6 (PR #4732) — unsafe conv | 1.39× | 1.05× |
| Fused FlyDSL VK (this PR) — safe conv, shipped default | 2.03× | 1.53× |
| Fused FlyDSL VK (this PR) — unsafe conv (`AITER_FAST_FP32_TO_FP16=1`) | 2.24× | 1.70× |

**Relation to recent work**

| PR | Relation to this PR |
|---|---|
| #4598 |  Complementary, but not overlapping. It fuses the front of the pipeline; this PR fuses the back. Together they take GDN prefill from six kernels to two. |
| #4683|  Same K5+K6 topology, different pipeline. FlashKDA serves `chunk_delta_attn/` (per-channel `gk`, BT=32); this PR serves `gated_delta_rule/prefill/` and picks up KDA shapes only when `flash_kda_supported()` declines them. |
| #4741  |  `gfx950`-only. Corroborates the design from this PR. Its numbers show the fully-fused K1–K6 is losing to the prep/scan split. Supports the decision for fusing at the K5+K6 boundary and points against folding the preprocessing in. Not portable as-is: it uses `mfma_f32_16x16x32_bf16` (gfx950-only) and assumes 160 KB LDS vs gfx942's 64 KB. |
| #4353  | Initial port of the HIP K5 kernel on FlyDSL - similar to K5-only path in this PR. Differs mainly in regard of LDS usage and number barriers needed in scheduling interleaved operations. |
| #4732  | Optimized version of HIP K5 port | 

This PR is gfx942-native: every choice below (MFMA shape, LDS budget, transposing LDS reads) follows from CDNA3 constraints that the gfx950 kernels do not have. On the other hand, the K5 kernel from this PR is more optimized towards MI300X and MI325X than the version from PR #4732. Also, the K5+K6 kernel from this PR is the only gfx942 kernel that provides K5 + K6 fusion.

## Technical Details

**One kernel, two modes.** `chunk_gated_delta_h_gfx942.py` builds both the K5-only and the fused
kernel from one source, switched by a `COMPUTE_OUTPUT` compile-time flag. The fused build pairs
with `STORE_H=False` / `SAVE_NEW_VALUE=False`, which is what elides the two HBM drains.

The fusion is possible because K6's operands are already in LDS at the end of K5's chunk body:

| LDS buffer | Holds | K6 consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `lds_h` | the `h` snapshot (state *before* this chunk's update) | GEMM3 B-operand |
| `lds_kt` | `k` | GEMM4a B-operand |
| `lds_vnt` | the gated `v_new`, `[BV, BT]` | GEMM4b B-operand |
| `lds_w` | dead after GEMM1 → restaged as `q` | GEMM3 / GEMM4a A-operand |

The subtlety worth reviewing: GEMM3 needs the *pre-update* snapshot, which works only because
`lds_h` still holds it while GEMM2's result lives in registers and is never written back within
the iteration.

**LDS is the binding constraint.** Five buffers at `BT=64, K=128, BV=64` total exactly 64 KiB —
the gfx942 limit — which pins the kernel to one workgroup per CU. `q` reuses `lds_w` rather than
taking its own buffer; an `lds_A`-onto-`lds_h` aliasing path exists for configurations that would
otherwise overflow.

**Kernel instance selection is two closed-form rules.**

- *Which K5/K5+K6 instance* — This is driven by `H*N` (number of heads `x` number of sequences): 
`H*N <= 32 → bv16`, `H*N<= 80 → bv32`, `H*N> 80 → bv64w8`.
- *Fused vs separate* — fuse iff `ceil(V/BV)·N·H / CU >= 0.45`, where `BV` is the V-axis tile size of the instance 
that the heuristics selected.  In other words, used fused instance when it fills the device sufficiently.

**MI308 path is unchanged.** gfx942 covers MI300A, MI300X, MI308X, and MI325X . 
The CU count (`_device_cu_count()`) is used to discriminate between different chips: MI300X/MI325X have 304 CUs
while other chips have less. The `elif use_chunk_flydsl` branch in `chunk.py` routes to `chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h_flydsl`
(VK kernel, this PR) only when `_device_cu_count() >= 304` and no flydsl_opt-only features are in use
(indexed state pool via `initial_state_indices`, `inplace_final_state`, or non-default `snapshot_dtype`).
All other callers (including every MI308 call path) fall back to `chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h_flydsl_opt`,
preserving existing behavior.

**Bounds handling — reads and writes.** Every token-indexed read (`k`, `q`, `w`, `u`, `g`, `gk`)
uses a buffer descriptor rooted at the CTA's `(sequence, head)` with an exact `T_local` extent, so
a row past the sequence end is out of range of the descriptor and the hardware returns zero. 

The `v_new` and `o` **stores** are bounded by the same construction: a write past `num_records` is
discarded by the hardware, so the padding rows of a partial last chunk store nowhere and the
per-element tail guards on both stores are gone as well. 

**f32 → bf16 conversion.** `arith.truncf` (IEEE round-to-nearest-even), which preserves NaN and
Inf classification by construction. A faster non-NaN version is available as an
explicit opt-in, `AITER_FAST_FP32_TO_FP16=1`, which is ~15% faster on K5 and ~11% on the fused kernel,
but does **not** preserve NaN. Both are covered by a direct converter unit test.

**Other kernel work in this PR:** 
- tiled copy / tiled MMA throughout
- XCD chiplet remapping so CTAs sharing `k`/`w`/`gate` land on the same die (L2 hit rate improvement)
- cheap `f32→bf16` rounding path (gfx942 lacks `v_cvt_pk_bf16_f32`)
## Test Plan

Two suites move from `op_tests/flydsl_tests/` to `op_tests/`. 
After the move both suites are picked up by the standard `aiter-test` shards.

| Suite | Status | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `op_tests/test_flydsl_linear_attention_prefill.py` | moved + **augmented** | K5 correctness vs a pure-PyTorch reference across gates, GQA/MHA, varlen and ragged batches; plus the variant-selection rule as pure-function tests.  Trimmed down the test suite for CI execution. The original test suite can be executed by running with `full_grid` option. Performance tests are also executed separately.|
| `op_tests/test_flydsl_gdn_fused_k5k6.py` | moved + **new in this PR** | Fused output vs `PyTorch-K5-ref → Triton-K6`; final-state check; end-to-end pipeline under `fusion=ALWAYS` vs the Triton baseline; the H·N tile rule and the fill-based routing rule; an auto-routing test that asserts the routing decision. |
| `op_tests/test_flydsl_bf16_convert.py` | **new in this PR** | Direct f32→bf16 converter probe: low-payload/signaling/quiet NaNs, all-ones-mantissa NaN, ±Inf, ±0, FLT_MAX, rounding tie.  |

Both suites also carry the perf sweep as a `__main__` entry point, so the benchmark and the
correctness test exercise the same input builders

## Test Result

**Unit / integration — CI should show these green.** Locally on MI325X (gfx942):

runs with `output_final_state=True`, so all five do the same work. The results are reproducible by
running `op_tests/op_benchmarks/flydsl/bench_gdn_fused_k5k6.py`.

#### MI325X — Standalone K5

`flydsl_opt` is the optimized HIP port from PR #4732; `flydsl_vk` is this PR, reported in both

title: [Triton/Gluon] [gfx1250] fp8_mqa_logits: fix epilogue store masks for cu_start != 0
[Triton/Gluon] [BENCHMARK] Adding utility function for torch profiler based benchmarking
body:
## Motivation

Currently, triton benchmarks rely on triton.testing.do_bench but its defaults are not very accurate isolating per kernel times. This PR introduces a new bench. utility that uses torch profiler under the hood and can better strip out the wrapper overhead. Under cuda-graph, the wrapper overhead is rarely seen in traces so measuring actual kernel time provides a more accurate signal.

It also supports l2 cache flushing and rotating buffers to simulate cold cache runtime.

I changed the profiler for bench_fp8_mqa_logits.py to the new one to use as an example.
 ## Technical Details
Adds `do_bench_profiler()` in `op_tests/op_benchmarks/triton/utils/profiler_bench.py`. It runs `fn` under `torch.profiler`, keeps only the device events whose name matches one of the kernel names you pass, groups the launches back into iterations and reduces across them. Returns per-iteration milliseconds, same unit as `do_bench`, so it drops into existing scripts without rescaling.

- `num_warmup` / `num_iters` are literal iteration counts, not `do_bench`'s ms budgets.
- `flush_l2` (on by default) with `cache_size_mb` (512).
- `data_gen` + `num_copies` build rotating input sets up front as an alternative to flushing. Iteration `i` gets copy `i % num_copies`, called as `fn(*data)` for a tuple, `fn(**data)` for a dict, else `fn(data)`.
- `return_mode` takes mean/median/min/max or any percentile (`p25`, `p50`, `p90`, ...). Pass a list to get several statistics out of a single run instead of re-benchmarking per statistic. `RETURN_MODES` is exported for use as argparse choices.
- `per_kernel=True` returns a dict keyed by filter name rather than the aggregate, which is the multi-kernel breakdown.

title: [Triton/Gluon] Fix int32 overflow in _gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle_varctx K/scale load offset
body:
## Motivation
The VarCtx gluon kernel `_gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle_varctx`
loads K/scale with `gl.amd.cdna3.buffer_load`, whose voffset is a **32-bit**
element offset. The block index (`context_kv_idx`, int32) is multiplied by
`stride_k_seq` while still int32, so for a wide paged cache the product
`block_index * stride_k_seq` crosses `2**31` and wraps. The load then reads out of
bounds and returns 0, so whole logit segments silently collapse to `0` for the
sequences that own high block indices (large batch). This PR loads K/scale with
64-bit pointer arithmetic via `gl.load`, matching the non-VarCtx preshuffle path.

### Issue
`deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits(..., Preshuffle=True, VarCtxSchedule=<schedule>)`
produces wrong output — whole segments become exactly `0.0` — at large batch with
variable context lengths on MI355X / gfx950. The non-VarCtx SplitKV path
(`VarCtxSchedule=None`) is always correct.

### Root cause
`stride_k_seq = kv_cache_fp8.stride(0) = KVBlockSize * index_dim`. The paged cache
row is `KVBlockSize * (head_dim + 4)` bytes — the extra 4 fp32-scale bytes per
block make the row stride **non-power-of-two**, e.g. `64 * (128 + 4) = 8448`
(not `64*128 = 8192`).

`context_kv_idx` is int32, and `gl.amd.cdna3.buffer_load` takes a **32-bit**
offset. The offset `context_kv_idx * stride_k_seq` therefore overflows once

```
block_index * 8448 >= 2**31  ->  block_index >= 2**31 / 8448 = 254201
```

The wrapped offset lands outside the buffer, the hardware buffer bound makes the
load return 0, and the resulting logits are `relu(q·0)·w = 0`.

<!-- Explain the purpose of this PR and the goals it aims to achieve. -->

## Technical Details

<!-- Explain the changes along with any relevant GitHub links. -->
For each of the 4 K/scale load pairs in the `LoadBlockIndiceForEachStage == True`
branch (the `KVBlockSize=64` path used by the c4 indexer), switch from
`buffer_load(ptr=..., offsets=... int32 ...)` to `gl.load(ptr + ... int64 ...)`:

```python
# before (int32 offset -> overflow at block_index*stride_k_seq >= 2**31):
k_next_0 = gl.amd.cdna3.buffer_load(
    ptr=KV_buffer,
    offsets=offset_k_fixed + context_kv_idx_next_0[None, :] * stride_k_seq,
)
# after (64-bit pointer arithmetic, cannot overflow):
k_next_0 = gl.load(
    KV_buffer
    + offset_k_fixed
    + context_kv_idx_next_0.to(gl.int64)[None, :] * stride_k_seq
)
```

Same change for `k_next_1` and the two `k_scale_f_next_*`
(`context_kv_idx.to(gl.int64) * stride_scale_seq`). This mirrors exactly what the
non-VarCtx `_gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` kernel already does.
## Test Plan
`op_tests/test_pa_mqa_logits_varctx_overflow.py` builds a distinct-per-sequence
paged cache (`block_tables = arange`) with `batch=256` and variable ctx so the
global block index crosses 254201, asserts the config actually reaches the
`2**31` boundary, then checks the VarCtx output against the known-good SplitKV
path: (1) no valid position is zeroed where SplitKV is non-zero, and (2) per-row
`cos(VarCtx, SplitKV) > 0.999`.
<!-- Explain any relevant testing done to verify this PR. -->

## Test Result
Test on (gfx950 / MI355X)
| kernel | test |
|---|---|
| before (buffer_load, int32) | **FAIL** — `VarCtx zeroed 51576 valid logits in row 254` |
| after (gl.load, int64) | **PASS** |

<!-- Briefly summarize test outcomes. -->

## Submission Checklist

- [ ] Look over the contributing guidelines at https://github.com/ROCm/ROCm/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-requests.

title: [Triton/Gluon] [Kimi-K3][ROCm] Add merged MoE front
body:
## Summary

Adds a merged MoE-front kernel for Kimi-K3 on gfx950, plus tuned GEMM
configurations and numerical tests for it.

Kimi-K3's MoE front is three separate projections of the same `x[M, 7168]`:
shared gate/up `7168 -> 1536`, router logits `7168 -> 896`, and the routed
latent `7168 -> 3584`. This kernel combines them into one
`BF16 x BF16 -> FP32` GEMM (`7168 -> 6016`) followed by a Triton split/SiTU
epilogue that emits the BF16 shared SiTU intermediate, the FP32 router logits,
and the BF16 routed latent. Routed experts are untouched and still use the
existing AITER MXFP4 backend.

## Supported shapes

```text
1..16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112, 128, 192, 512, 1024, 1536, 2048
```

`32..192` is the MTP decode bucket. A pure-decode step submits
`num_seqs * (1 + num_speculative_tokens)` tokens, so with the usual
`num_speculative_tokens=3` any server past four concurrent sequences asks for a
count above 16. The gate itself lives in the companion vLLM change; what this
PR adds for those shapes is numerical coverage, since the decode test
previously stopped at `m=16`.

`kimik3_bf16_tuned_gemm.csv` gains FP32-output entries at `N=6016, K=7168,
gfx950, cu_num=256` for `M = 7, 14, 16, 512, 1024, 1536, 2048`. Config lookup
is keyed on output dtype and pads `M` up to the next multiple of 16 below 256,
so every `M` in `1..16` resolves to the `M=16` entry. The `32..192` bucket has
no FP32-output entry yet and therefore runs on torch's default hipBLASLt
heuristic; the end-to-end numbers below already include that fallback, so
tuning those shapes is remaining headroom rather than a prerequisite.

`M=4096` and `M=8192` are intentionally excluded after controlled retesting
showed regressions.

## Kernel results

Single-GPU gfx950, complete front, CUDA Graph:

| M | Speedup vs native front |
|---|---:|
| 1..16 | 1.645x – 2.140x |
| 512 | 1.224x |
| 1024 | 1.185x |
| 1536 | 1.162x |
| 2048 | 1.129x |
| 4096 | 0.960x, excluded |
| 8192 | 0.882x, excluded |

All tested shapes pass numerical checks, including exact router top-16
selection.

## End-to-end results

MI355X, TP8, DSpark MTP (`num_speculative_tokens=3`), via the companion vLLM
change. Both arms of each comparison ran back to back on one node with
identical server arguments, KV configuration and client invocation.

### 8K/1K fixed sequence length

ISL 8192, OSL 1024, prefix caching disabled, 610 requests per arm, zero
failures.

| Concurrency | Decode M | Output throughput | Median TPOT |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 130.1 -> 135.9 tok/s, **+4.43%** | 7.15 -> 6.83 ms, **-4.53%** |
| 4 | 16 | 369.9 -> 380.5 tok/s, **+2.87%** | 9.25 -> 8.97 ms, **-2.98%** |
| 8 | 32 | 582.8 -> 606.5 tok/s, **+4.07%** | 11.99 -> 11.31 ms, **-5.66%** |
| 16 | 64 | 799.8 -> 814.3 tok/s, **+1.82%** | 18.00 -> 17.65 ms, **-1.98%** |
| 32 | 128 | 1030.2 -> 1044.7 tok/s, **+1.41%** | 28.95 -> 28.55 ms, **-1.37%** |

Median TTFT moves by at most 0.58% in any cell: prefill in this workload is
8130-8190 tokens per step and never matches a supported shape, so the gain is
decode-only. Repeating two of these rows independently bounds their
reproducibility at 0.13-0.80 pp.

### AgenticX trace replay, 3600 s per cell

| Metric | C1 | C4 |
|---|---|---|
| Total throughput | 10212 -> 10533 tok/s, **+3.14%** | 19211 -> 19617 tok/s, **+2.11%** |
| Output throughput | 84.77 -> 87.75 tok/s, **+3.52%** | 139.20 -> 146.61 tok/s, **+5.33%** |
| P90 TPOT | 8.92 -> 8.47 ms, **-5.03%** | 13.52 -> 13.36 ms, **-1.19%** |
| P90 interactivity | 112.1 -> 118.1 tok/s, **+5.29%** | 73.9 -> 74.8 tok/s, **+1.20%** |

Read the total-throughput row with care: it does not measure this change.
Input tokens are over 99% of all tokens in this trace and 97.6% of them hit the
prefix cache, so total throughput is close to (input tokens handed to this arm)
/ wall clock. Trace replay assigns sessions dynamically and the two arms did
not get an identical token mix -- the optimized arm received 3.04% more input
tokens at C1 and 2.81% more at C4. Dividing the measured total-throughput delta
by each arm's input-token and duration ratio leaves a residual of +0.00% at C1
and +0.02% at C4, so that row is token mix and nothing else.

Output throughput and P90 TPOT are the rows that carry the effect: both are
normalized per output token, so neither depends on how much input the arm
happened to receive. Note that they disagree in shape with the total row at C4,
where output throughput is +5.33% against a total of +2.11% -- the smaller
number there is the noisier one, not the more conservative one.

## Accuracy

GSM8K, full 1319-question test split, 5-shot, greedy. This is the check the
numerical tests structurally cannot make: they compare the fused kernel against
a `torch.mm` reference built from the same merged weight, so they are blind to
the merged front slicing its router logits out of a `7168 -> 6016` accumulator
where the native front runs a separate `7168 -> 896` GEMM. Both are
BF16 x BF16 -> FP32, but the wider shape picks a different solution with a
different accumulation order, and that rounding difference can flip a borderline
top-16 expert selection.

Both arms ran back to back on one node at `max_num_seqs=8` with
`num_speculative_tokens=3` and block rejection sampling, so a saturated decode
step submits 32 tokens and the merged front is the decode path for effectively
the whole run.

| Filter | Baseline | Merged |
|---|---:|---:|
| strict-match | 0.9659 | 0.9719 |
| flexible-extract | 0.9651 | 0.9712 |

Both arms answer the same questions, so the paired view is the informative one:
1295 of 1319 answers agree, 16 flip to correct and 8 flip to incorrect, an exact
two-sided sign test on the 24 discordant pairs giving p = 0.15. The merged front
is therefore indistinguishable from the native front on accuracy. The +0.6 pp is
run-to-run nondeterminism, not a claimed improvement.


## Validation

- Ruff (`ruff==0.16.0`, the version `pre-checks.yaml` pins), `ruff format` and
  `git diff --check`: passed. The two `EXE001` findings that remain in the
  repository are in unrelated flydsl files and predate this PR.
- gfx950 AITER tests: `17 passed`.
- Dependent vLLM Kimi-K3 tests: `59 passed`.

Companion vLLM PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55811
